(p-91) (Surat al-Hajj is Madani except verses [52, 53, 54, 55], which are Meccan (between Mecca and Medina); its verses number 78.)

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord⁠﴾ This is an address whose ruling encompasses the responsible persons (al-mukallafun) at the time of revelation, and whoever will later be included among them from those who exist but have not yet reached the rank of legal responsibility (al-qasirin 'an rutbat al-taklif), and those who come into being after that until the Day of Resurrection. Although the direct address (khitab al-mushafahah) is specific to the first group, in the manner whose explanation has passed at the beginning of (Surat al-Nisa'). The word "al-nas" (mankind) genuinely includes both males and females. As for the form of the masculine plural, it comes in the way of taghlib (predominance of the masculine), since it does not literally cover females, except according to the Hanabilah. The command is to general taqwa (God-consciousness), which is avoiding everything that makes one sinful, whether of action or omission. It includes belief in Allah and the Last Day, as the Shari'ah has reported, by primary inclusion. The mention of the title of Lordship (al-rububiyyah), which indicates ownership (al-malikiyyah) and nurture (al-tarbiyah), together with its attribution to the pronoun of those addressed, serves to reinforce the matter and to emphasize the obligation of compliance with it, through both warning and encouragement. That is: beware of the punishment of the Owner of your affairs and your Nurturer.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing⁠﴾ This is a justification for the requirement of the command, by mentioning some of its terrible punishments. For observing its greatness, its awfulness, and the horror of what are its beginnings and preliminaries, from conditions and terrors from which there is no refuge except by clothing oneself in the garment of taqwa, necessarily calls for greater attention to adhering to it and persisting in it. Zalzalah (convulsion) is a violent shaking and vehement agitation by way of repetition, to the extent that it removes things from their places and dislodges them from their positions. Its attribution to al-Sa'ah (the Hour) is either the attribution of the verbal noun to its agent by way of metaphor in the judgmental sense, as if it were the Hour itself that shakes things; or its attribution to the time expression, either by treating it as an object in a broadened sense, or by the implied presence of "fi," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, the scheming of the night and the day⁠﴾. This is the zalzalah mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake⁠﴾. From al-Hasan: that it will occur on the Day of Resurrection. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: the zalzalah of the Hour is its establishment (qiyamuha). From 'Alqamah and al-Sha'bi: that it will be before the sun rises from its west, so its attribution to the Hour is then because it is one of its portents. The expression of it as "a thing" indicates that intellects fall short of grasping its essence, and that expression is too narrow to encompass it except in a manner of vagueness.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿On the Day you see it﴾ is in the accusative, governed by what follows it, and it has been placed first for emphasis. The pronoun refers to the earthquake (zalzalah), meaning: at the time of your seeing it and witnessing the terror of its appearance.

﴿Every nursing mother will be distracted﴾, that is, every woman actively nursing, ﴿from what she was nursing﴾, that is, she will be heedless, in bewilderment, of the one she was about to nurse from her own child, whom she had put to her breast. The expression "what" (mā) rather than "whom" (man) is used to stress the distraction and that her state is such that it does not occur to her what he is, not that she knows his identity but does not know who he is specifically. It has been said that "mā" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle, meaning: she will be distracted from her nursing. The first reading is more indicative of the intensity of the terror and the completeness of the alarm. It has been read as "tudhhal" (from al-idhhal), in the passive, or in the active with "kull" in the accusative, meaning: the earthquake will distract them.

﴿And every pregnant woman will drop her burden﴾, that is, she will cast her fetus before its completion, just as the nursing mother is distracted from her child before weaning. This is evident according to the view of ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbi. As for what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it has been said that it is a figure of speech to magnify the matter; and in this there is the implication that the matter is then even more severe, greater, more terrifying, and more overwhelming than what has been described. It has been said that this will occur at the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah), for they will rise from what they were struck by in the first blast, so the nursing mother will rise to her nursing and the pregnant woman to her carrying. There is no doubt that the people's rising from their graves after the second blast, not before it, is what would allow what has been mentioned to be conceived.

﴿And you will see people﴾ read with the letters tā' and rā' open, addressing each one of the addressees with the seeing of the earthquake. The difference in plurality and singularity is because the object seen in the first is the earthquake, which all witness, while in the second it is a state of those other than the addressee among them; so it is necessary to make the addressee singular in a way that encompasses each one of them, but without considering his being characterized by that state, for the purpose is to show the effect of the earthquake on the one seen, not on the one who sees, through differing feelings, because its basis is the aspect of his seeing the earthquake and not something else. As if it were said: "and the people will become drunk," etc.; but what is in the revelation was preferred to it to indicate the complete manifestness of that state in them and its reaching such clarity that it hardly escapes anyone, that is, everyone sees them.

﴿Drunken﴾, that is, as if they were drunk, ﴿yet they are not drunk﴾ in reality, ﴿but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾, so its terror overwhelms them, dazes their minds, and strips them of discernment; it is He who made them as they have been described. It has been read "turā" with the tā' open and the rā' open, ascribed to the addressee from "araytuka qā'iman" or "ruʾyatuka qā'iman," with "the people" in the accusative, meaning: you think them drunk. It has been read with "the people" in the nominative, the verb being passive, and the feminine form in view of the group. It has been read "tarā" with the tā' open... [sic] — with the tā' pronounced with damma and the rā' with kasra, meaning: the earthquake shows the creation, all people, to be drunk. It has been read "sakrā" and "sakrā," like ʿaṭshā and jawʿā, treating drunkenness as an affliction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 3:

﴿وَمِنَ النّاسِ﴾ (And among the people) is a new (independent) sentence, introduced after the great emphasis on the magnitude of the Hour, which announces the Resurrection, as an explanation of the condition of some of those who deny it. The place of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wal-majrur) is nominative (raf') by way of being the subject of a nominal clause (ibtida'), either by treating it according to its meaning, or by estimating what it relates to, as has been mentioned many times; that is: "and some of the people," or "and some who are among the people."

﴿مَن يُجادِلُ في اللَّهِ﴾ (who disputes concerning Allah): that is, concerning His Majesty, and says about Him what is not good, of falsehoods.

And His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾ (without knowledge) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yujadilu," clarifying what the disputing implies of ignorance; that is: accompanied by no knowledge. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was a disputer; he would say that the angels are the daughters of Allah, that the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients, and that there is no resurrection after death. And it is general in application to him and to his likes among the rebellious tyrants.

﴿وَيَتَّبِعُ﴾ (and follows): that is, in what he undertakes of disputation, or in everything he does and leaves undone of false matters, of which this is part.

﴿كُلَّ شَيْطانٍ مَرِيدٍ﴾ (every rebellious devil): obstinate, rebellious, stripped bare for corruption. Its root is the bare arm, which indicates readiness for it, like rolling up one's sleeves; perhaps it is taken from the stripping of wrestlers during wrestling. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Marid and al-Marid is the high, smooth (thing)." The intended meaning is either the leaders of the disbelievers who call others to disbelief besides Allah, or Iblis and his soldiers.

**Translation**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It was decreed for him﴾, that is, for Satan, is another qualifying clause (ṣifah) describing him. His saying, Exalted is He: "that" (*annahu*) is the grammatical subject (*fā'il*) of *kutiba* (it was decreed), and the pronoun (*ḍamīr*) refers to the matter (*al-sha'n*), meaning: it was recorded for him, because his condition makes it evident that the matter is that [he will be misled].

﴿Whoever takes him as a patron﴾, that is, takes him as a friend (*walī*) and follows him, ﴿then he will lead him astray﴾. It is read with a *fatḥah* on the *hamzah* (*fa-annahu*), on the basis that it is the predicate (*khabar*) of an elided subject (*mubtada'* *maḥdhūf*), or a subject whose predicate is elided. The clause is the apodosis (*jawāb al-sharṭ*) if *man* is taken as a conditional particle (*sharṭiyyah*), and it is its predicate if *man* is taken as a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*) containing the meaning of the condition. That is, whoever takes him as a patron, his state is that he will mislead him away from the path of Paradise or the path of truth; or, the meaning is: it is certain that he will mislead him without doubt. It has been said that *fa-annahu* is conjoined (*ma'ṭūf*) to *annahu*, but this involves a great deal of strained construction (*ta'assuf*), which is obvious. It has also been said that this view is not free from contrivance (*tamaḥḥul*) and forced interpretation (*ta'wīl*).

It was also read as *fa-innahu* with a *kasrah*, on the basis that it is the predicate of *man* or its apodosis. It was read with a *kasrah* in both places on the basis of quoting what was written (*ḥikāyat al-maktūb*), as in your saying: "I wrote: Indeed Allah commands justice and excellence." Or it is on the basis of an implied verb of saying (*iḍmār al-qawl*), or on the basis of treating *al-kutub* (writing) as containing its meaning (*taḍmīn*), according to the view of those who hold that position.

﴿And guides him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾, by making him engage directly in what leads to it of misdeeds.

﴿O mankind﴾. After describing the state of those who dispute without knowledge, and pointing to their eventual outcome, the proof establishing the reality of what they disputed, namely the Resurrection (al-ba'th), is presented.

﴿If you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾, whether as to its possibility and its being within the power of God, exalted is He, or as to its occurrence. It has been read as ﴿min al-ba'th﴾ with a vowel on the middle letter (bi-l-taharruk), like "jalab" for "jalb". The expression of their belief concerning it as "doubt", with the indefinite form that indicates little (of doubt), although they are certain of its impossibility, and the use of the word for doubt (shakk) despite the establishment of their condition in that regard, and the preference for the wording of the noble Text over saying "if you doubt the Resurrection", have already been investigated in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾.

﴿Then indeed We created you﴾, i.e., consider the origin of your creation so that your doubt may disappear. ﴿Indeed We created you﴾, i.e., We created each individual of you ﴿from dust﴾ within the creation of Adam from it, a creation in summary. For the creation of each individual of mankind has a share in his creation, peace be upon him, when his noble natural disposition (fitrah) is not confined to himself, but was a prototype (unmudhaj) enfolding the natural dispositions of all members of the species in a summary enfolding, entailing the operation of their effects upon all. Thus his creation, peace be upon him, from dust was a creation of all of them from it, as has been investigated repeatedly.

﴿Then from a drop﴾, i.e., then We created you in a detailed creation from a drop, that is, from semen, from among the drops, which is the pouring forth.

﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾, i.e., a piece of congealed blood formed from the semen. ﴿Then from a lump of flesh﴾, i.e., a piece of flesh formed from the clot, which in origin is the amount that is chewed.

﴿Formed (mukhallaqah)﴾, with the genitive, is an adjective of "lump", i.e., with its creation distinct and its form shaped.

﴿And unformed (ghayr mukhallaqah)﴾, i.e., its creation and form have not yet become distinct. The intent is to detail the state of the lump: that at first it was a piece in which none of the limbs had appeared, and then they appeared gradually, one after another. The preceding sequence, based on gradation from remote beginnings to near ones, required that the unformed be mentioned before the formed; it is placed after it because the unformed is the absence of the faculty (adam al-malakah). Moreover, these two have been explained as "shaped and unshaped", and as "complete and fallen", but this is not the right explanation. In making each of these stages a beginning for their creation, and not for the creation of the stages that follow them, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then We made the drop a clot, then We made the clot a lump﴾ ... the verse, there is greater indication of the immensity of His power, exalted is He, and a breaking of the force of their incredulous rejection.

﴿That He may make clear to you﴾ is connected with ﴿We created﴾. The object is omitted to magnify it in quantity and quality, i.e., We created you in this wondrous pattern so that We may make clear to you by it what expression cannot encompass of realities and subtleties, among which is the secret of the Resurrection. For whoever deeply reflects upon the gradual creation mentioned, with genuine reflection, will be certain with necessary certainty that He who originated humans first from dust, which had never smelled the scent of life, and who fashioned them in a manner suitable for producing their like again and again, by directing them through the stages of creation and transforming them from one state to another despite the contrariety and difference between those stages and states, is capable of restoring them. Indeed, He is easier by analogy, considering the agent and the recipient. It has been read as ﴿li-yubayyina﴾ (that He may make clear), by way of iltifat (the grammatical shift from one person to another).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will﴾ form a resumptive statement (isti'naf) directed toward explaining their state after the completion of their creation. The non-arrangement of this and what is conjoined to it within the series of creation that is explained by "making clear", although they are among its completions and also among its beginnings of making clear, is because the indication of the first (creation) of the complete power of God, exalted is He, over all things capable of being done, of which the Resurrection under discussion is one, is clearer and more manifest. That is: and We cause to remain in the wombs thereafter what We will to cause to remain in them.

﴿Until a specified term﴾: this is the time of delivery, and its least is six months and its greatest two years. It has been said: four years. In this is an indication that some of what is in the wombs God, exalted is He, does not will to remain in them after its creation is complete, so it miscarries. Discussing abortion (izlaq) does not suit the present context, since the discussion concerns what the stages of creation pass through. This is explicit that by "unformed" is not meant one who is born deficient or defective, and that what has been detailed up to here are the stages that successively befall the child before birth. It has been read as ﴿yuqirru﴾ with the ya', and ﴿nuqirru﴾ and ﴿yaqurru﴾ with a damma on the qaf, from qarrat al-ma', when you pour water.

﴿Then We bring you forth﴾, i.e., from the bellies of your mothers after your remaining in them, when the specified term is complete.

﴿As children (tifl)﴾, i.e., while you are children. The singular is used with reference to each one of them, or by intending the collective kind which includes the one and the many. It has been read as ﴿yukhrijukum﴾ with the ya'.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then that you may reach your maturity (ashudd)﴾ are a purpose clause for ﴿We bring you forth﴾, conjoined to another purpose clause for it that is suitable to it, as if it were said: then We bring you forth so that you may grow gradually, then so that you may reach your full strength, intellect and discernment. It has been said that the estimated sense is: then We grant you respite so that you may reach... etc. What has been said, that it is conjoined to ﴿We make clear﴾, undermines the eloquence of the noble arrangement. Moreover, the two preceding verbs have been read in the subjunctive, in narrative (hikayah) and third person form, so it is then conjoined to ﴿nubayyin﴾ like them, and the meaning is: We created you in the said gradation for two ends following upon it: one, that We may make clear Our affairs; the second, that We cause you to remain in the wombs, then bring you forth as children, then that you may reach your maturity. The placement of the making clear before what follows it, although its actual realization occurs after all of them, is to announce that it is the ultimate end and intended in itself. The repetition of the particle of purpose here, while the first two are stripped of it, is to indicate its primacy as a purpose in relation to them, since upon it revolves the obligation (taklif) leading to happiness and misery. The choice of "reaching" (bulugh) attributed to the addressees, rather than "making reach" (tabligh) attributed to Him, exalted is He, like the preceding verbs, is because it is more suitable to showing their state of attaining perfection and their independence in being principles of effects and actions. ﴿Ashudd﴾ (maturity) is one of the plural forms for which no singular has been used, like "asad" (lions) and "qutud" (saddles). It is as if, when it was an intensity in something that had no (other) thing, it was formed on the plural form.

﴿And among you is one who is taken back (yutawaffa)﴾, i.e., after reaching maturity or before it. It has been read as ﴿yatawaffa﴾ in the active voice, i.e., God, exalted is He, takes him.

﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age (ardhal al-'umur)﴾, which is senility and decrepitude. It has been read with the mim vowel-less (sukun). The use of "returned" and "taken back" in the passive form is in accordance with the custom of majesty, to avoid specifying the agent.

﴿So that he does not know, after knowing, anything﴾: i.e., after much knowledge, ﴿anything﴾, i.e., anything of things, or anything of knowledge, as an exaggeration in the diminishment of his knowledge and the reversal of his condition, i.e., that he returns to what he was at the time of childhood, with weakness of body, feebleness of intellect and scarcity of understanding, so that he forgets what he knew, denies what he recognized, and is incapable of what he was able to do. In this there is, as is not hidden, an alert to the validity of the Resurrection.

﴿And you see the earth lifeless (hamidah)﴾: this is another proof of the validity of the Resurrection. The address is to every person who is able to see. The present tense form indicates renewal and continuity. It is visual sight. ﴿Hamidah﴾ is a state (hal) of the earth: i.e., dead and dry, from "hamadat al-nar", when it becomes ash.

﴿Then when We send down upon it water﴾, i.e., rain, ﴿it stirs (ihtazzat)﴾, moves with vegetation, ﴿and swells (rabat)﴾, expands and increases. It has been read as ﴿rabaʾat﴾, i.e., it rose.

﴿And it causes to grow of every kind (zawj)﴾, i.e., category, ﴿beautiful (bahij)﴾, good, pleasing, which delights its beholder.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 22, verse 6:**

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ is a resumptive statement (*kalam mustaʾnaf*, a sentence that begins a new point while connected to what precedes it), brought after establishing the truth of the Resurrection and presenting proof for it from the two worlds of humankind and plants. It serves to show that this is among the effects of His divinity (*ulūhiyyah*) and of the judgments of His essential, attributive and active affairs. It also shows that what they deny, not merely its existence but even its possibility, namely the coming of the Hour and the Resurrection, is among the causes of those wondrous effects that they witness in themselves and in the horizons, and among the origins of their emergence from Him, exalted is He. In this there is an announcement of the strength of the proof, and the root of what is indicated is established in verification, and it shows clearly the falsity of their denial. For denying the realization of the cause while being certain of the realization of the effect is something that the self-evident truths of reason (*badihat al-ʿuqul*) judge to be false.

By "the Truth" is meant the one whose existence is necessarily established, because it is essential to Him and not merely the existent in an unrestricted sense. "That" is a reference to what was mentioned of the creation of humans in various stages, His directing them through different conditions, and the reviving of the earth after its death. The sense of distance in it serves to announce the distance of His rank in perfection. It is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is the prepositional phrase, meaning: that wondrous act occurs because He, exalted is He, is the Truth alone in His essence, attributes and acts, the one who establishes all other things.

﴿And that He gives life to the dead﴾: that is, it is His affair and custom to revive them. The sum of it is that He, exalted is He, is capable of reviving them, both at the beginning and in return; otherwise He would not have revived the drop of semen and the dead earth repeatedly, time after time. What the present tense indicates of renewal is only with respect to the connection of the power and its object, not with respect to the power itself.

﴿And that He is capable of all things﴾: that is, He is emphatically powerful. Otherwise He would not have brought into existence these existents, which are perishing, and among which is what has been mentioned. As for the argument for this by saying that His power, exalted is He, is due to His essence, which relates to all things equally, so that when observation shows His power over reviving some of the dead, it necessarily follows that He is capable of reviving all of them, the source of heedlessness regarding what the noble composition was brought to explain is that the mentioned final effects are branches and effects of the general and comprehensive power. The specific mention of reviving the dead, although it is among the things over which He has power, is for the explicit statement of what is in dispute and what the deniers oppose, and its placement first is to highlight the concern with it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 7:

﴿And that the Hour is coming﴾ i.e., in what is to come. The choice of the active participle (ātiyah) over the verb is to indicate the certainty of its coming and to affirm it definitively, since wisdom necessitates it without doubt. Its rationale, that change is among the preliminaries and harbingers of cessation, is based on what has been mentioned of heedlessness.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ is either a second predicate (khabar) of "anna" or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "the Hour" in the predicate. The meaning of negating doubt about it is: its matter is so manifest and its evidences, both cosmic (takwiniyyah) and revealed (tanzīliyyah), so clear that there is no likelihood of doubting its coming, as has passed in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The clause is conjoined to the object of the preposition "bi" (ba'), like the two clauses preceding it, and falls, like them, within the scope of causation (sababiyyah). Likewise His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿and that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves﴾, but not in the sense that the coming of the Hour and the resurrection of the dead are effects in the way that His actions mentioned are effects of power; rather, in the sense that each of them is a cause that calls for Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, by the demand of His mercy toward the servants, which is grounded in profound wisdoms, up to what has been mentioned: the creation of them and the reviving of the dead earth in a wondrous pattern suitable for being cited as evidence of their place, so that they may reflect on that, infer from it their certain occurrence, believe in what the clear revelation declares about them, and attain eternal happiness through it. Were it not for that, He, exalted is He, would not have done what He did; indeed, He would not have created the world at all. This, as you see, is among the rulings of His truth (haqqiyyah) in His actions and their being founded upon manifest wisdoms, just as what precedes it is among the rulings of His truth in His attributes and their being in utmost perfection. The coming of the Hour and the raising of those in the graves have been made, because they are among the followers (rawadif) of wisdom, a metonymy (kinayah) for His being Wise, as if it were said: that is because He, exalted is He, is capable of reviving the dead and of every possible thing, and He is Wise, who does not break His promise, and He has promised the Hour and the resurrection, so He must fulfill what He promised. You should know that its ultimate implication is inference from His wisdom to the coming of the Hour and the resurrection, and the discourse is not about that; rather, it is about their being a cause for what has passed of the creation of man and the reviving of the earth. So reflect, and be upon the manifest truth.

It has been said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that the Hour is coming﴾ is not conjoined to the object of the preposition "bi" (ba'), nor does it fall within the scope of causation; rather, it is a predicate, and the subject is omitted for understanding of the meaning, the estimate being: "and the matter is that the Hour is coming," and the second "anna" is conjoined to the first. It has also been said: the meaning is: that is so that you may know that Allah is the Truth ... the two verses.

﴿Among the people is one who argues about Allah﴾: he is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It was also said: he is anyone who sets himself up to mislead people and lead them astray, whoever he may be, just as the first (Abu Jahl) is one who follows them, and "the devil" is an expression for the misleader and seducer in the absolute sense.

﴿without knowledge﴾: this is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in "argues," meaning: while being without knowledge. By "knowledge" is meant necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri), just as by "guidance" in His statement, ﴿and no guidance﴾, is meant reasoning (al-istidlal) and sound inquiry (al-nazar al-sahih) that leads to knowledge.

﴿and no enlightening Book﴾: a revelation (wahy) that manifests the truth. That is, he argues about the matter of Allah, the Exalted, without holding to a necessary premise, without a theoretical proof, and without a transmitted (sam'i) evidence, as in His statement, ﴿And they worship besides Allah what He has not sent down any authority for, and about which they have no knowledge﴾. As for what has been said, that the intended meaning is the first argument and that the repetition is for emphasis and as a preparation for what follows, namely the explanation that it has a basis of either reasoning or revelation, this is not supported by the noble arrangement of the text. How could it be, when describing him as following every devil, described as having the features mentioned, already suffices in place of describing him as devoid of rational and transmitted proof?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 9:

﴿ثانِيَ عِطْفِهِ﴾ is another circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a phrase describing the state of the subject) referring to the doer of "يُجادِلُ" (yujādilu, "argues"). It means: inclining his side, bending his flank, turning away arrogantly and disdainfully. Bending the flank (thany al-ʿiṭf) is a kināya (metonymy) for arrogance (al-takabbur). It was also read with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, "عَطْفِهِ" ('aṭfihi), meaning: preventing his own bending (towards others).

﴿لِيُضِلَّ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ is connected to "يُجادِلُ". His aim is to lead people astray from it, even if he does not admit that it is misguidance. The meaning of "يُضِلَّ" (yuḍilla, "to lead astray") is either: removing (people) from guidance into error, in which case the object of "يُجادِلُهُ" (yujādiluhu, "argues with him") is the believers or people in general, with the believers given precedence (taghlīb, prioritization of one group over another) over others; or: keeping (people) fixed in error or increasing it, figuratively (majāz), in which case the object is the disbelievers specifically. It was also read with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, "يَفْضِلَ"? No: it was read with a fatḥa on the yāʾ of "يُضِلَّ" as "يَضِلَّ" (yaḍilla, "he goes astray"), and his going astray is made the consequence (ghāya) of his arguing, since the intended meaning is manifest error with no guidance after it, while he had been able to attain guidance before that.

﴿لَهُ في الدُّنْيا خِزْيٌ﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumla mustaʾnafa) brought to explain the outcome of the path he took. It means: there becomes established for him in this world, because of what he did, disgrace (khizy), which is what befell him on the day of Badr of killing and humiliation.

﴿وَنُذِيقُهُ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ عَذابَ الحَرِيقِ﴾ That is, the blazing Fire.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ That, i.e., what has been mentioned of the worldly and otherworldly punishment, and what it contains of the sense of distance (*bu'd*), to indicate that it is at the farthest extreme of terror and awfulness. It is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿بِما قَدَّمَتْ يَداكَ﴾ *because of what your hands have sent forward*, i.e., because of what you committed of disbelief and sins. Attributing it to "his two hands" is because acquisition (*iktisab*) usually takes place through the hands, and the shift (*iltifat*) in address is to emphasize the warning and intensify the threat.

The place of "*anna*" in His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿وَأنَّ اللَّهَ لَيْسَ بِظَلامٍ لِلْعَبِيدِ﴾ *and that God is not unjust to the servants*, is nominative (*raf'*), as the predicate of an elided subject, i.e., "and the matter is that He, Exalted is He, does not punish His servants without any sin on their part." Expressing this by negating injustice, although punishing them without sin is not injustice at all by the established principle of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), let alone being gross injustice, is due to the fact that its verification has already passed in (Surat Al 'Imran). The sentence is a concluding parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraDh tadhyili*) confirming the content of what precedes it. As for what has been said, that the place of "*anna*" is genitive (*jarr*) by coordination with "*ma qaddamat*", its status has already been explained in (Surat al-Anfal).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 11:

﴿And among people is one who worships Allah upon an edge﴾. This begins the description of the wavering ones (al-mudhabdhabin) after the description of the openly hostile. That is: among them is one who worships Him, exalted is He, on the fringe of the religion, seeking some benefit from it, like one who veers toward the edge of the army: if he senses victory he advances, and otherwise he flees.

﴿If good befalls him﴾, i.e., worldly good of health and abundance, ﴿he is content with it﴾, i.e., he remains outwardly upon what he was upon. It does not mean that he is content with it in the manner of the believers, whom no diverting obstacle turns away and no inclination restrains.

﴿But if an ordeal befalls him﴾, i.e., something by which he is tested, of a disagreeable kind that afflicts him in his person, his family, or his property.

﴿He turns over upon his face﴾. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Bedouin (a'arib) who came to Medina. One of them, when his body was healthy, his mare foaled a fine foal, his wife bore a sound child, and his wealth and livestock increased, would say: "Since I entered this religion of mine, I have encountered nothing but good," and he would be content. But if the matter were otherwise, he would say: "I have encountered nothing but evil," and he would turn away. And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him: "That a Jew embraced Islam, then calamities befell him, so he blamed Islam for ill omen, and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Release me from it.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, Islam is not to be abandoned,' and then this was revealed." It was also said: it was revealed concerning those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum).

﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter﴾, i.e., he has lost and wasted both of them, by the departure of his protection and the nullification of his deeds through apostasy. It is read "khasira" (خاسِرَ) in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), and in the nominative (raf') as the fā'il (subject), and the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to emphasize his loss; or it is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence).

﴿That﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned of loss, and the sense of distance contained in it indicates that it is at the utmost degree.

﴿That is the clear loss﴾, i.e., its being a loss is evident, for there is no loss like it. (p-98)

﴿يَدْعُو مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement) explaining the magnitude of the loss. That is: he worships, going beyond the worship of Allah the Exalted, ﴿that which does not harm him﴾ if he does not worship it, ﴿and that which does not benefit him﴾ if he worships it. That is, [they are] inanimate objects whose nature does not include harm or benefit, as the repetition of the word "ما" (*mā*, "that which") hints.

﴿That﴾ calling ﴿is the far error﴾ from the truth and guidance. It is a metaphor (*mustaʿār*) drawn from the error of one who is driven far off into the wilderness, straying from the path.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 13:**

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes it), brought to explain the outcome of the calling mentioned, and to establish that it is far-gone error. It also removes what might be suspected, namely that harm is denied of the object of worship only directly, by also denying it indirectly (by way of causation). So "yad'u" (he calls) is in the sense of "he says," and the lām (the lam of address) enters on the clause that is the object of the saying. "Man" (مَن, whoever) is the subject, and "ḍarruhu" (ضَرُّهُ, his harm) is a second subject, whose predicate is "aqrabu" (أَقْرَبُ, nearer). The clause is a relative clause (ṣila) for the first subject.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely wretched is the protector, and surely wretched is the companion﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, and the oath with its answer is the predicate of the first subject. The choice of "man" (مَن) over "ma" (مَا, what), although his object of worship is inanimate, and the use of the comparative form (ṣīghat al-tafḍīl) although it is entirely devoid of benefit, are for emphasis in disparaging his state and in thoroughly censuring him. That is: on the Day of Resurrection that disbeliever will say, with calling and shouting, when he sees the harm done to him by his object of worship and his entering the Fire because of it, while no trace of benefit from it is seen at all: "By Allah, surely wretched is the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit as a helper, and surely wretched is he as a companion!" How then with what is pure harm, utterly devoid of benefit?

It is also permissible that the second "yad'u" (يَدْعُو) be a repetition of the first, not merely for emphasis (tawkid), but also as a preparation for what follows of the explanation of the bad state of his object of worship, after the explanation of the bad state of his worship. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the far-off error﴾. It is as if it were said, on His part, exalted is He, after mentioning his worship of what neither harms him nor benefits him: "He calls upon that," then it was said: "to one whose harm is nearer than his benefit: surely wretched is the protector, and surely wretched is the companion!" So the word "man" and the comparative form are for mockery of him.

It was also said: the lām is superfluous (zā'ida), and "man" (مَن) is the object of "yad'u" (يَدْعُو). This is supported by the reading without a lām, that is: "he worships whose harm is nearer than his benefit." The use of the word "man" and the comparative form is also mockery of him, and the oath clause is resumptive.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 14:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), brought to explain the perfection of the good condition of the believers who worship Him, the Exalted, and that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestows upon them favours beyond which there is no limit, the most excellent benefits and the greatest good, following the explanation of the extreme evil condition and final state of the disbelievers from the two groups of those who openly oppose (al-mujahirin) and those who waver (al-mudhabdhabin). It also explains that the object of their worship does not avail them anything of benefit; rather it harms them with a great harm, and that they acknowledge the evil of its guardianship and companionship and blame it with a general blame.

His, the Exalted, statement ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is an attribute of "gardens." If by them is meant the dense trees that shade what is beneath them, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident. If by them is meant the land, then an elision of a modifier (mudaf) must be assumed, (p-99) i.e., "from beneath their trees." If it is taken as an expression for the whole of the land and the trees together, then the consideration of being "beneath" is with regard to the visible part, which justifies applying the name "garden" to the whole, as its detailed explanation has passed at the beginning of (Surat al-Baqarah).

His, the Exalted, statement ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾ is a justification of what precedes it and an affirmation of it by way of confirmation, i.e., He definitely does every deed He wills, from among the perfectly executed and fitting actions, founded upon refined wisdoms, of which among them is rewarding those who believe in Him and affirm His Messenger (ﷺ), and punishing those who associate others with Him and deny His Messenger (ﷺ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 15:

Since this is among the effects of God's support for him (ﷺ), the Exalted and Majestic One followed it with His words: ﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter...﴾, to confirm it and establish its firmness in the most emphatic and forceful manner. In this there is a masterful brevity and a wonderful conciseness. The meaning is: God is certainly the helper of His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter, without any diverting force turning Him away or any inclination causing Him to hesitate. So whoever is enraged by this on account of his enemies and envious rivals, and thinks that God will not do it because of his resisting some matters and engaging in the schemes that repel it, let him exert himself to the utmost and strive beyond every known limit. For the ultimate outcome of his plotting and the end of his scheming is that he will choke with rage at what he sees of the failure of his endeavors and the non-fruition of his premises and beginnings.

﴿Then let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾: let him stretch a rope to the ceiling of his house. ﴿Then let him cut off﴾: that is, let him choke, for one who chokes cuts off his breath by blocking its passages. It has also been said: let him cut the rope after being choked, with the meaning that the cutting is hypothetical and assumed, just as the meaning of "looking" in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then let him look: does his scheming remove that which enrages him?﴾ is the assumption and depiction of looking, i.e., let him picture in his own mind the look: does his scheming remove that which is the furthest reach of his power in the domain of opposition and harm, namely what enrages him of the support, entirely? It is also permissible that the meaning be: let him now look at whether, if he does that, it removes what enrages him. It has also been said: the meaning is, let him stretch a rope to the canopied sky and climb upon it, then let him cut off the revelation. It has also been said: let him cut the distance until he reaches its limits, then strive to repel His support. But this is rejected, because the context of the noble composition is to explain that the matters assumed to occur and be realized are far removed from removing what enrages. It is clear that there is no sense in assuming the occurrence of impossible matters and ordering the looking upon it, especially the cutting off of revelation, for assuming its occurrence certainly undermines the purpose.

It has also been said: some Muslims, out of intense rage and fury at the polytheists, were growing impatient with the support God and His Messenger (ﷺ) had promised, while others among the polytheists wished to follow him (ﷺ) and feared that his affair would not be firmly established, so this verse was revealed. The word "support" has also been interpreted as "provision," and the meaning then is: sustenance is in the hand of God, the Exalted, and cannot be obtained except by His will, so the servant must be content with His distribution. Whoever thinks that God is not his provider, and does not endure patiently or submit, let him reach the utmost limit of distress, which is choking, for that does not overcome the allotment nor cause it to return him unprovided for.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 16:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., like that wondrous sending down, which contains profound wisdoms, ﴿We sent it down﴾, i.e., the entire Noble Qur'an. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿as clear signs﴾, i.e., evident in their indication of their refined meanings, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the accusative position, explaining what was pointed to by ﴿that﴾.

﴿And that Allah guides﴾ by it from the outset, or keeps firm in guidance, or increases in it, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to be guided (p-100) or to be kept firm or to be increased in it. The place (i'rab) of the clause is either in the genitive, by elision of the governing particle attached to an omitted word placed later, i.e., "and because Allah guides whom He wills, He sent it down thus," or in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "and the matter is that Allah guides whom He wills to guide."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of the clear signs, by the guidance of God Most High, or in everything that one must believe in, so that what has been mentioned enters it as a primary inclusion. ﴿And those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians﴾. It has been said: they are a people who worship fire. It has been said: they worship the sun and the moon. It has been said: they are a people from among the Christians who withdrew from them, wore woolen garments, and took something from the religion of the Christians and something from the religion of the Jews. And they are the ones who say that the world has two principles, light and darkness.

﴿And those who associate partners﴾ are the worshippers of idols.

And His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is in the place of nominative case, as the predicate of the preceding "inna" (indeed). The opening of both clauses with the particle of affirmation serves to increase the confirmation and emphasis. That is: He will decide between the believers and the five groups that adhere to the religion of disbelief, by manifesting the truthful from the falsehood and giving each of them its due recompense, rewarding the first and punishing the second according to the deserts of the individuals of each of them.

And His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God is over all things a witness﴾ is a justification for what precedes it of the judgment, that is: He is knowing of all things and observant of their conditions. And among the requirements of this is His encompassing knowledge of the details of what proceeded from each individual of the groups mentioned, and His executing upon him the recompense befitting him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ and so on, is an explanation of what necessitates the aforementioned separation, from the deeds of the aforementioned groups, along with an indication of its manner and that it is by way of punishment, reward, honour and humiliation, following the explanation of what necessitates it, namely that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things, of which their states and actions are a part. By "seeing" is meant knowledge; it is expressed by it to indicate the manifestation of the known, and the address is to everyone who is capable of seeing, on the basis that it is of such clarity that it is hidden from no one. By "prostration" is meant complete submission to His, exalted is He, governance, by way of metaphor founded on likening it to the most perfect acts of the obligated in the matter of obedience, signifying that He is at the utmost degrees of subjugation and humility, not the prostration of worship that is specific to the rational. This applies whether the word "min" (whoever) is taken as general, including non-rational beings as well, and this is the more fitting to the context, since it conveys the inclusion of the wisdoms for everything in them, by way of being settled in them or by way of being a part of them. Then His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, and the animals﴾ would be a singling out of them by mention because of their fame and the unlikelihood of that from them ordinarily. Or it is taken as specific to the rational, since the prostration of obedience does not include all of them, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and many of mankind﴾. For it is raised by a hidden verb indicated by what was mentioned, meaning: and many of mankind prostrate to Him, the prostration of obedience and worship, and it follows from this that this is negated for some of them. It has been said: it is raised as the subject of a sentence whose predicate is omitted, relying on the predicate of its counterpart to indicate it, such as "the reward is due to him." The first is preferable, because of what it contains of encouragement toward prostration and obedience. It has also been permitted that ﴿from mankind﴾ be its predicate, meaning: from among mankind those who are truly mankind, namely the righteous and the God-fearing; and that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and many﴾ be conjoined to the first "many," to indicate the extreme of abundance, then He informs about them that they deserve punishment, as if it were said: and many of mankind.

﴿The punishment is justly due to him﴾, meaning: because of his disbelief and defiance. It was also read as "ḥaqqa" with a ḍamma, and "ḥaqqan," meaning: the punishment is due to him, truly.

﴿And whoever Allah humiliates﴾ by having wretchedness written for him, as He knew him to divert his choice toward evil, ﴿then there is none to honour him﴾ with felicity. It was also read with a fatḥa on the rā', as a mīmī verbal noun.

﴿Indeed Allah does what He wills﴾ of things, of which honour and humiliation are a part.

﴿هَذانِ﴾ ("These two") specifies the two parties of the dispute and removes any doubt that might arise, namely that it lies between each of the six groups and the rest. It also clarifies its location, i.e., the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, which is divided into five groups. 50 ﴿خَصْمانِ﴾ ("two adversaries") means two disputing parties. The phrase ﴿اخْتَصَمُوا في رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("they dispute concerning their Lord") is in the plural because of the sense of the word (فَرِيقانِ, "two parties"), i.e., they dispute concerning His affair, the Mighty and Majestic. It is also said: concerning His religion; and it is said: concerning His essence and attributes. All of these are among His affairs, exalted is He. The belief of each of the two parties that what it holds is true and what its opponent holds is false, and the building of its statements and actions upon that belief, is a dispute with the other party, even if no actual debate or contention takes place between them.

It is also said: the Jews and the believers disputed. The Jews said: "We are more entitled to God than you, and our Book is older than yours, and our Prophet came before your Prophet." The believers said: "We are more entitled to God than you. We believed in Muhammad and in the Prophet of yours, and in what God has sent down of Book, while you know our Book and our Prophet, then you disbelieved in him out of envy." So this was revealed.

﴿فالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("As for those who disbelieve") is an elaboration of what was stated in summary in His saying: ﴿يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ ("He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection").

﴿قُطِّعَتْ لَهُمْ﴾ ("garments of fire will be cut out for them") means: they will be measured according to the sizes of their bodies. It is also read with the lighter pronunciation (قُطِّعَتْ, as qaṭṭa'at with tashdid removed).

﴿ثِيابٌ مِن نارٍ﴾ ("garments of fire") means: mighty fires that surround them, encompassing them as garments encompass the one who wears them. ﴿يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ الحَمِيمُ﴾ ("boiling water is poured over their heads") means: scalding water whose heat has reached its extreme. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "If a single drop of it were dripped onto the mountains of this world, it would melt them."

The sentence is either a new independent clause, or a second predicate of the relative pronoun (الَّذِينَ), or a circumstantial clause (حال) from the pronoun in ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ ("for them").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 20:

﴿Whereby there shall be melted﴾, i.e., dissolved, ﴿that which is in their bellies﴾ of the intestines and the entrails. It is also read as "yuṣahhar" with the doubled letter (tashdid).

﴿And the skins﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "mā" (that which), and its placement after it is either for the sake of observing the rhyme-endings (fawasil), or to convey an impression of the extreme intensity of the heat, by giving the impression that its effect on the interior comes before its effect on the exterior, even though their contact is the reverse. The clause is a circumstantial phrase (ḥal) referring to "al-ḥamīm" (the boiling water).

﴿And for them﴾, i.e., for the disbelievers, that is, for their punishment and their appointed term, ﴿are maqāmi' of iron﴾. The word مَقامِع is the plural of مَقْمَعَة, which denotes the instrument of qam' (subduing, beating down).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 22:

﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it﴾ i.e., they approach getting out of the Fire and draw near to it, according to what is related: it strikes them with its flames and lifts them up, until when they are at its top, they are struck with maqami' (iron hooks), and they fall back into it, for seventy autumns (kharif).

﴿out of distress﴾ i.e., out of severe distress from its distresses. It is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion) from the pronoun (in "minha"), with the preposition repeated, and the connecting pronoun (rabit) is elided as has been indicated. Or it is a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose) for "to get out."

﴿They will be returned into it﴾ i.e., into its depths, by being sent back from its heights to its lowest parts, without getting out of it.

﴿And taste﴾ is governed by an implied verb of saying, conjoined to "they will be returned," i.e., it will be said to them: taste ﴿the punishment of the burning﴾, i.e., the intense fire that spreads and is great in destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. This is an explanation of the good condition of the believers following the explanation of the bad condition of the disbelievers. The style has been changed here by attributing the admission to Allah, glory be to Him, and by beginning the sentence with the particle of emphasis (ḥarf al-taḥqīq), to signal the complete contrast between their condition and the condition of the disbelievers, to show greater care for the matter of the believers, and to indicate the certainty of the content of the statement.

﴿They will be adorned therein﴾ is in the passive form, with doubling, from al-taḥliyah (adornment). It was also read with the single-consonant form, from al-iḥlā' (meaning "to clothe"), i.e., the angels will adorn them by His command, may He be exalted. It was also read "yuḥallawna" from the adornment of a woman when she puts on her jewelry. The "min" in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿of bracelets (min asāwira)﴾ is either partitive, i.e., "some bracelets," asāwir being the plural of uswira, which is the plural of siwār; or explanatory, since the mention of adornment indicates an unspecified ornament; and it was said that it is superfluous; and it was said that it is an adjective of an omitted object of "yuḥallawna," for it has the meaning of "they will wear."

﴿of gold (min dhahab)﴾ is an explanation of the bracelets. ﴿And pearls (wa-lu'lu'an)﴾ is conjoined to the position (maḥall) of "min asāwira," or to the omitted object, or it is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "yuḥallawna," i.e., "they will be given." It was also read in the genitive, conjoined to "asāwira." It was read "lu'lu'an" with the second hamza changed to a waw, and "lūlīyan" with it changed to a yāʾ after changing both to waw, and "laylīyan" with both changed to yāʾ.

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾: the style has been changed here, since He did not say "and they will wear silk therein," but not in order to indicate that silk is their customary garments, nor merely to preserve the form of the verse endings (fawāṣil). Rather, it is to signal that the existence of clothing for them is a certain matter, needing no explanation, since it is not possible for them to be without it; what needs explaining is what their clothing is. By contrast, bracelets and pearls are not among the necessary essentials, so the description of their adornment with them was made a primary purpose. And perhaps this is the reason I placed the description of the adornment before the description of the state of their clothing.

And they were guided to the good word, which is their saying: "All praise is for God, who has fulfilled His promise to us and caused us to inherit the earth, that we may dwell in the Garden wherever we will..." (the verse).

And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid). That is, the Praiseworthy may mean the One who is praiseworthy in His own essence, or His outcome, which is the Garden. The reason this guidance is mentioned after the guidance to the aforementioned speech, which comes after entering the Garden, and that entering comes after the guidance to its way, is for the sake of observing the rhyme of the verse endings (fawasil). It has also been said that the intended meaning of "al-Hamid" is the Truth that deserves all praise in its very essence, which is God, Mighty and Majestic, and His path is Islam. The reason for the delay in this case is that the mention of praise calls for the mention of the One who is praised.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ The intended meaning here is neither the present nor the future; rather, it is the continuation of the barring. For this reason, its conjunction (ʿatf) to the past tense is appropriate, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "disbelieved," meaning: "while they bar." The predicate of "inna" (indeed) is omitted, because the end of the noble verse indicates it. For if one who commits wrongdoing (ilḥād) in the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram) is punished with a painful torment, then it is more fitting and more appropriate that one who combines disbelief with barring from the way of Allah be punished with something even more severe than that.

﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾ is conjoined to "the way of Allah." It has been said that what is meant by it is Makkah, as evidenced by His description of it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which We have made for the people﴾, i.e., whoever he may be, without distinction between a resident of Makkah and an outsider (āfāqī).

﴿equal are the one who dwells therein and the visitor﴾, i.e., the one who resides and the one who comes passing through. "Sawāʾ" means "equal," i.e., level; it is the second object of "jaʿalnāhu" (We made it), and "al-ʿākif" (the dweller) is raised by it, and the preposition "lām" (for) is attached to it as an adverbial complement. The benefit of describing the Sacred Mosque with this is to intensify the reproach of those who bar others from it. It has also been read as "sawāʾun" in the nominative, as a predicate preceding its subject, with "al-ʿākif" as the subject, and the clause is the second object of "al-jaʿl." It has also been read "al-ʿākifi" in the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for "al-nās" (the people).

﴿And whoever intends therein﴾, its object having been omitted so that it encompasses every kind of intending, as if it were said: "And whoever intends therein any intention at all."

﴿with deviation﴾, by turning away from the right course, ﴿with wrongdoing﴾, without right. These two are synonymous circumstantial clauses (ḥālān mutarādifān), or the second is a substitute for the first by repeating the preposition, or it is a complement; i.e., deviating through the cause of wrongdoing, such as associating partners with Allah and committing sins.

﴿We shall make him taste of a painful punishment﴾ is the response (jawāb) to "man" (whoever).

﴿And [mention] when We settled﴾. It is said: "He settled him (bawwa'ahu) in a dwelling (manzilan)," meaning he lodged him in it. When the first party stayed in the place, the second made the place a dwelling-place (mubā'ah) for the first. It was said: ﴿for Abraham, the place of the House﴾. On this basis is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the verb is "ja'alnāhu" (We made it). The meaning is: "Remember the time when We made the place of the House a dwelling-place for him, peace be upon him," that is, a place to which he would return for its upkeep (al-'imārah) and worship. The command to remember is directed at a time, although the intended purpose is to recall the events that occurred in it. This has been explained more than once. It was also said that the lam (lām) is superfluous (ziyādah), and that "makān" (place) is an adverbial of place (ẓarf), as in its original usage, meaning: "We settled him in it."

It is said that God raised the House to heaven during the days of the Flood. It had been made of red ruby. God informed Abraham, peace be upon him, of its location by means of a wind that He sent, called al-Khujūj, which swept clean what was around it. He then built it upon its ancient foundation.

It is related that the Noble Ka'bah was built five times. The first was the building of the angels, and it was of red ruby; then it was raised during the days of the Flood. The second was the building of Abraham, peace be upon him. The third was the building of the Quraysh in the pre-Islamic era (al-Jāhiliyyah), and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ attended this building. The fourth was the building of Ibn al-Zubayr. The fifth was the building of al-Ḥajjāj. We have set out what is said on this matter in the commentary on His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾.

The "an" (أن) in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿that you associate nothing with Me﴾ is either explanatory (mufassirah) of "bawwa'nā" (We settled), insofar as the verb contains the sense of "ta'budunā" (worship Us), since the settling was for worship; or it is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle joined to the prohibition. Its verification has been discussed at the beginning of Surah Hud. That is: "We did this so that you would not associate anything with Me in worship."

﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate﴾. That is: purify My House from idols and filth for whoever circumambulates it and prays in it. Perhaps the expression of prayer by its constituent parts (arkān) is to indicate that each of them independently requires this, so how much more so when they are combined. It is also read as "yushrik" (يُشْرِكُ) with a ya' (ي), so that the verb is in the third person.

﴿And proclaim among the people﴾, that is, call out to them. It was read as "adhān" (أذانٌ).

﴿with the Hajj﴾, with the call to the Hajj and the command to perform it. "It is narrated that he (ﷺ) ascended Abu Qubays and said: 'O people, perform the Hajj to the House of your Lord.' So God the Exalted made hear him whoever was in the loins of men and the wombs of women, between the east and the west, of those whom He foreknew would perform the Hajj." It was said that the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who was commanded with this during the Farewell Pilgrimage, but the fact that the surah is Meccan rejects this.

﴿they will come to you﴾ is the answer to the command. ﴿on foot﴾, that is, walking, the plural of "rājil," like "qiyām," the plural of "qāʾim." It was read as "rujāl" with a ḍamm on the rāʾ and with the jīm either lightened or doubled, and as "rajālā," like "ʿajālā."

﴿and upon every lean camel﴾ is conjoined to "rijālan." That is: and riding, upon every camel that has become lean, which the long journey has wearied so that it became lean, or whose leanness increased.

﴿they come﴾ is an attribute of "ḍāmir" (lean camel) taken according to its meaning (the feminine plural "yaʾtīna" agrees with the sense of the plural camels, though the word is singular). It was read as "yaʾtūna," which makes it an attribute of the men and the riders, or a resumptive new sentence (istiʾnāf), in which case the pronoun refers to the people.

﴿from every deep ravine﴾: "fajj" is a wide path, and "ʿamīq" is distant. It was read as "maʿīq." It is said: a well is "baʿīdat al-ʿumq" (far in depth) and "baʿīdat al-muʿq," with the same meaning, like "al-jadhb" and "al-jabdh" (both meaning drawing or pulling).

﴿لِيَشْهَدُوا﴾ (*li-yashhadu*, "that they may witness") is connected to ﴿يَأْتُوكَ﴾ ("they come to you"), not to ﴿أذِّنْ﴾ ("proclaim"). That is, "so that they may attend." ﴿مَنافِعَ﴾ (*manafi'a*, "benefits") means benefits of great importance and great number, or a kind of religious and worldly benefit specific to this worship. The lam in His words, ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ ("for them"), is connected to an omitted verb that serves as an adjective to ﴿مَنافِعَ﴾. That is, "benefits that belong to them."

﴿وَيَذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("and that they may mention the name of God") refers to mentioning it when preparing the offerings and the sacrificial animals and slaughtering them. Making it the purpose of the coming indicates that it is the supreme goal, not any other. It has also been said that it is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for slaughter, since mentioning the name is inseparable from it.

﴿فِي أيّامٍ مَعْلُوماتٍ﴾ ("on known days") are the days of sacrifice (*nahr*), as indicated by His words, ﴿عَلى ما رَزَقَهم مِن بَهِيمَةِ الأنْعامِ﴾ ("over what He has provided them of the cattle beasts"). The mention intended is what occurs at the time of slaughter. It has also been said that they are the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. The verb has been tied to the thing provided, and it is specified as "the beasts," to encourage drawing near (to God) and to alert to the mention (of God's name).

﴿فَكُلُوا مِنها﴾ ("so eat from it") is a shift to the address (*iltifat*). The fa is an eloquent fa (*fa' fasiha*), linking what follows it to an omitted premise, which has been dropped to convey that the matter is certain and does not need to be stated explicitly, as in His words, ﴿فانْفَجَرَتْ﴾ ("so it gushed forth"). That is: "Mention the name of God over your sacrificial animals, so eat from their meat." The command is for permission, and to remove the scruple that the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) had regarding it. Or it is for recommendation (*nadb*) toward comforting the poor and sharing with them.

﴿وَأطْعِمُوا البائِسَ﴾ ("and feed the distressed"), that is, the one who has been struck by misery and hardship.

﴿الفَقِيرَ﴾ ("the poor"), the one in need. This command is for obligation (*wujub*), and it has been said that the first command also carries this meaning.

Then let them complete their rites (tafath), that is, let them remove their dirt (wasakh), or let them accomplish it by trimming the moustache and nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair at the time of ihlal (exiting the state of ihram).

And let them fulfill their vows (nudhur), that is, what they vow of righteous deeds in their pilgrimage. It was also said: the obligatory duties of the Hajj. It has also been read as wa-liyawwafū, with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the fa'.

And let them circumambulate (yattawwafu) the Ancient House (al-bayt al-'atiq), meaning the circumambulation of the pillar (rukn) by which the exit from the state of ihram is completed, for it accompanies the fulfilment of the tafath. It was also said: the farewell circumambulation (tawaf al-wada').

The Ancient House (al-bayt al-'atiq) means the old one, for it is the first house set up for mankind; or the one freed (mu'taq) from the domination of tyrants, for many a tyrant marched against it intending to demolish it, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, broke him. As for al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, he only intended to expel Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, from it, not to dominate over it.

(p-105) ﴿That﴾: the matter is that, and this and the like, is used to separate two statements or two aspects of a single statement. ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾: that is, His rulings and everything whose violation is not permitted, by knowing that it is obligatory to observe them and by acting upon what they require. It was also said: the sanctuary (al-Haram) and what pertains to the pilgrimage of obligation (al-hajj) among the duties. It was also said: the Ka'bah, the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred City and the sacred months.

﴿then it is better for him﴾: that is, honouring them is better for him in reward ﴿with his Lord﴾: that is, in the Hereafter. The mention of the title "Lord" (rubbubiyyah), together with its attribution to the pronoun of "whoever," is to honour him and to indicate the reason for the ruling.

﴿And the livestock has been made lawful for you﴾: these are the eight pairs in their general sense. Then the words of the Exalted: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾: that is, except what the verse of its prohibition recites to you. It is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from them, on the basis that "what" refers to what has been prohibited from them for a passing cause, such as carrion and what has been dedicated to other than Allah the Exalted. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), brought to confirm what precedes it, namely the command to eat and to feed others, and to ward off what might be suspected, that the state of ihram prohibits it as it prohibits game. It was not sufficient to explain that they are not of that category by restricting "livestock" to what was mentioned, namely the known sacrificial animals and offerings, so that there would be no need for the mentioned exception, since among them there is nothing prohibited for a passing cause, with certainty; this is in order to observe the good transition to what follows, the words of the Exalted: ﴿So shun the filth of the idols﴾. This is because it follows from what the words of the Exalted ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾ imply, namely the obligation to observe them and to avoid violating them. Since the explanation of the permissibility of livestock is among the motives for partaking of them, not among the beginnings of avoidance, He followed it with what requires avoiding the prohibited things. Then He commanded avoidance of what is the greatest of the sacred things. It is as if it was said: whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him; and the livestock are not among the sacred rites, for they are lawful to you, except what is recited to you of its prohibition, for that is among what must be avoided. So avoid what is the greatest of the matters that must be avoided.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿and avoid the word of falsehood﴾ are a generalisation after a specification, for the worship of idols is the head of falsehood. It is as if, when He urged the honouring of the sacred things, He followed that with a refutation of what the unbelievers were upon, of prohibiting the baḥā'ir (she-camels whose ears were slit) and the sawā'ib (animals released for the idols) and the like, and of fabricating against Allah the Exalted that He had ruled with that. It was also said: it refers to false testimony, on the basis of what has been narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "False testimony is equal to associating partners with Allah the Exalted," three times, and he recited this verse. The word zūr (falsehood) derives from zawr, which means deviation, like ifk (calumny), derived from ifk, which means turning and diverting, for falsehood is deviating and diverted from reality. It was also said: it is the saying of the people of ignorance in their talbiyah (call of pilgrimage): "Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he possesses."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 31:

﴿Hunafa'a lillah﴾ (inclining away from every deviant religion toward the true religion, sincerely devoted to Him, exalted is He), ﴿ghayra mushrikina bihi﴾ (not associating anything with Him). That is, not associating anything of things with Him, so that idols enter into this in the first place. These two phrases are circumstantial clauses (hal) relating to the waw in "fajtanibu" (so avoid).

﴿Wa man yushrik billah﴾ (And whoever associates partners with Allah) is an independent nominal clause (jumla mubtada'a) emphasizing what precedes it concerning avoiding association. The manifest use of the Glorious Name serves to show the ugliness of associating partners.

﴿Fa-ka'annama kharra min al-sama'﴾ (then it is as if he had fallen from the sky), because he has dropped from the height of faith to the depths of disbelief.

﴿Fa-takhtafuhu al-tayr﴾ (then the birds snatch him away), for destructive desires scatter his thoughts. It is also read "fa-takhattafahu" with a fatha on the kha' and a shadda on the ta', and with a kasra on the kha' and the ta', and with a kasra on the ta' along with a kasra on both, and its original form is "takhtatifuhu" (the verb is in the form that carries the notion of seizing repeatedly).

﴿Aw tahwi bihi al-rih﴾ (or the wind carries him off), that is, it casts him down and hurls him ﴿fi makanin sahiq﴾ (into a remote place), a far-off place, for Satan has flung him into error. (p-106) The "aw" here is for giving a choice, as in "aw ka-sayyib" (Q. 2:19), or for variety. It is also possible that this is from the category of compound simile, so the meaning would be: whoever associates partners with Allah, his soul has perished in a destruction resembling the destruction of one of the perishing ones.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 32:

﴿That﴾ means: the matter is that, or: they should comply with that.

﴿And whoever honours the symbols of Allah﴾ means: the sacrificial animals, for they are among the landmarks (ma'alim) and rites (sha'a'ir) of the Hajj, may He be exalted, as is indicated by His words, ﴿And the camels We have made for you among the symbols of Allah﴾. This reading is the most fitting with what follows. Honouring them means believing that offering them in sacrifice is among the most excellent acts of drawing near to Allah, and that one chooses them to be fine, fat, and very costly. It is narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) offered a hundred camels, among them a camel belonging to Abu Jahl with a gold nose-ring in its nose, and that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) offered a noble she-camel for which he was asked three hundred dinars."

﴿For indeed it﴾ means: indeed the honouring of them ﴿is of the piety of the hearts﴾, that is, it is one of the acts of those who possess piety of the heart. So these added words and the pronoun referring back to "whoever" have been omitted. Or: indeed the honouring of them arises from the piety of the hearts, and the specifying of it by the attribution (to the hearts) is because the hearts are the seats of piety, which, when it is firmly established and settled in them, its effect appears in all the other limbs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 33:

﴿Therein for you﴾, i.e., in the sacrificial animals, ﴿are benefits﴾, namely their milk, their offspring, their wool, and their riding, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the time of their slaughter, the giving of their meat in charity, and eating from it. ﴿Then their place of sacrifice﴾, i.e., the obligation of slaughtering them, or the time of slaughtering them, ending ﴿at the Ancient House﴾, i.e., at what is adjacent to it of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). And "thumma" (then) here indicates temporal or rank-based sequence, meaning: for you therein are worldly benefits until the time of their slaughter, then religious benefits, the greatest of them in benefit being their place of sacrifice, i.e., the obligation of slaughtering them, or the time of the obligation of slaughtering them, at the Ancient House, meaning ending at it. That said, it has been said: what is intended by the "rites" (sha'a'ir) is the rituals (manasik) of the Hajj and its landmarks, and the meaning is: for you therein are benefits in reward and recompense in performing the rituals and establishing the rites of the Hajj until a specified term, which is the end of the days of the Hajj, ﴿then their place of sacrifice﴾, i.e., the place where people exit their state of ihram, ﴿at the Ancient House﴾, i.e., ending at it, by circumambulating it with the Tawaf al-Ziyarah on the Day of Sacrifice after completing the rituals. So the attribution of "place" (mahall) to it is due to the closest connection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 34:

﴿And for every community We have appointed rites﴾ i.e., for every people of a religion, ﴿We have appointed a manasak (manasik, rite of worship)﴾ i.e., a means of worship and an offering by which they draw near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also read with a kasra on the sin, i.e., a place of nusuk (sacrifice), and the placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb is for specification, i.e., for every community among the nations We have appointed a manasak, not for some to the exclusion of others.

﴿that they may mention the name of Allah﴾ exclusively, to the exclusion of any other, and that they may dedicate their nusayka (sacrifice) to His noble Face. The appointing is explained by this, as an alert that the original purpose of the rites is the remembrance of the Worshipped One.

﴿over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle﴾ at the time of their slaughter. In this there is an alert that the offering must be from the cattle.

The address in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so your God is one God﴾ is to all, by way of predominance. The fa' (so) indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes, for His appointing a rite for every nation is among the things that point to His oneness, Exalted is He. It was said "one God" and not merely "one" because the intent is to show that He, Exalted is He, is one in His essence just as He is one in His divinity over all. The fa' in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so to Him submit﴾ indicates the consequence of the command to submit (Islam) that follows upon His oneness, Exalted is He. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the command is for restriction, i.e., since your God is one God, then devote to Him alone the drawing near or the remembrance, make it for His Face alone, and do not mix it with polytheism.

﴿And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾ a turning of the address away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), i.e., the humble or the sincere, for humility (ikhbat) is among the duties specific to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 35:
