﴿Those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ — from Him, exalted is He, because of the radiance of the rays of His majesty falling upon them.

﴿And those who are patient over what afflicts them﴾ — from the hardships of the obligations and the burdens of calamities. ﴿And those who establish the prayer﴾ — at its appointed times. It has been read with the accusative of "al-salata" (the prayer) on the assumption of the omitted nun (of the plural), and it has been read "wal-muqimina al-salata" (and those who establish the prayer), in accordance with the original form.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ — in the various channels of good.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 36:

﴿And the camels (al-budn)﴾. The word is read with a damma on the ba' and a sukun on the dal. It is also read with a damma on the dal, and both forms are plurals of badanah (a camel sacrificed as an offering). It is said that the original form is with a damma on the dal, as in khushub and khashabah, and that the sukun is a lightening of it. It is also read with a shaddah on the nun, following the pausal form (lafz al-waqf). The camel was named badanah because of the bulk ('izam) of its body, from the root b-d-n, badanah and badanah. Since the cow shares with it the validity of sacrifice on behalf of seven persons, through the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The camel is for seven and the cow is for seven," and the two were made in the Sharia one genus, its accusative position is governed by a hidden verb that explains it.

﴿We have made them for you﴾. It is also read in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), with the sentence as its predicate. His saying, ﴿among the signs of God﴾, meaning among the markers of His religion that God has legislated, is the second object of the verb "made," and ﴿for you﴾ is an adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) attached to it. His saying, ﴿in them there is good for you﴾, meaning benefits of religion and of this world, is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanifah) that confirms what precedes it.

﴿Mention the name of God over them﴾, by saying at the time of their slaughter: God is most great; there is no god but God, and God is most great; O God, from You and to You.

﴿Standing in rows (saffan)﴾, meaning standing, having arranged their forelegs and hind legs. It is read ṣawāfin, from ṣafana, said of a horse when it stands on three legs with the tip of the hoof of the fourth. This is because the camel's one foreleg is tied, so it stands on three. It is also read ṣawāfan, by replacing the nunation with the vowel of prolongation (ḥarf al-iṭlāq) at pause. It is also read ṣawāfī, meaning purified for the sake of God, the Mighty and Majestic. And ṣawāf is in the dialect (lughah) of those who make the yā' quiet with the prolongation, as in his saying:

*La'alli ara baqin 'ala al-hadathan*

﴿When their sides fall (wajabat junubuha)﴾, meaning they fall upon the ground. This is a metaphor for death. ﴿Then eat from them and feed the contented (al-qani')﴾, the one who is satisfied with what he has and with what is given to him without asking. This is supported by the fact that it is read al-qun' or al-sa'il, from qana'a ilayhi qunu'an, when one humbles oneself to him in asking.

﴿And the one who is in need (al-mu'tarr)﴾, meaning the one who presents himself to be asked. It is read al-mu'tari. One says 'arrahu, 'araahu, i'tarrahu and i'taraahu.

﴿Thus﴾, like that wondrous subjugation implied by His saying ﴿standing in rows﴾: ﴿We have subjected them to you﴾, despite their great bulk and the extremity of their strength, so that they do not resist you, until you take them submissive, make them kneel, hold them standing on their legs, and then stab them in their chests.

﴿So that you may give thanks﴾, meaning that you may thank Our bestowal upon you by drawing near (to Him) and by sincerity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 37:

﴿It is not their meat that reaches God, nor their blood﴾ — that is, it will not reach His good pleasure, nor will it be accepted by Him — ﴿their meat﴾ (p-108) of what is given in charity from it, ﴿nor their blood﴾ spilled by slaughter, insofar as they are meat and blood.

﴿But it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾ — but what reaches Him is the piety of your hearts, which calls you to comply with His command, to glorify Him, to draw near to Him, and to be sincere toward Him. It was said: the people of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) would smear the Ka'bah with the blood of their sacrifices, so the Muslims intended to do the same, and this was revealed.

﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾ — a repetition for the sake of reminder, and a reason given by His words: ﴿that you may glorify God﴾ — that is, that you may know His greatness through His power over what no one else is able to do, so that you may single Him out for magnificence. It was also said that this refers to saying the takbir (Allahu akbar) at the time of unlawful-to-lawful release (ihlal) or at slaughter.

﴿for having guided you﴾ — that is, He has guided you to the way of subjecting them and the manner of drawing near through them. The "ma" here is either verbal-masdarial (meaning "for His guiding you") or relative (meaning "for what He guided you to"), and "for" (ʿala) is connected to "glorify" because it contains the meaning of thanking.

﴿And give good news to the muhsinun (those who do good)﴾ — that is, the sincere in everything they do and abstain from in the matters of their religion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to firmly settle the hearts of the believers by explaining that Allah the Exalted is their helper against their enemies, to the extent that they will not be able to prevent them from performing the Hajj, so that they may devote themselves to performing its rites. The opening of it with the word of affirmation (kalimat al-tahqiq) serves to highlight the complete attention given to its content. The form of the verb (sigha al-mufaʿala), namely "yudafiʿu," is either for emphasis (li-l-mubalagha) or to indicate the repetition of the defending. For this form may be stripped of the sense of the act being mutual from both sides, so that its repetition remains as in practice (ka-ma fi al-mumarasa). That is, He exerts great effort in repelling the peril of the polytheists and their harm, of which obstructing the way of Allah is part, with the effort of one who contends in it, or He repels it from them time after time, according as their intention to harm the Muslims is renewed, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.﴾ It has also been read as "yadfaʿu" (yadfaʿu), with the object omitted.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾ It is a reason (taʿlil) for what is implied within the generous promise of a threat (waʿid) against the polytheists, and a notification (iodhan) that their repulsion by way of subjugation and disgrace, and the negation of love, is a metaphor (kinaya) for hatred. That is: Allah hates every treacherous one regarding His trusts (amanat), which are His commands and prohibitions, or regarding all trusts, most of which are [those] of an ingrate for His blessing. The intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha) in both of them is to explain that they are like this, not to restrict the hatred to the extreme of treachery and disbelief, nor for emphasis in negating love according to the consideration of negation or not; and the bringing of the meaning of emphasis a second time.

﴿أُذِنَ﴾ means: it was permitted (ruḵḵiṣa). It is also read with the verb in the active form (al-binā' lil-fā'il, the grammatical active voice), meaning: God Most High permitted ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُقاتَلُونَ﴾, that is, those whom the polytheists fight against. The permitted action is omitted, since the mentioned part indicates it: the polytheists' fighting against them clearly points to their fighting against the polytheists. It is also read in the form of the active-voice verb (al-mabnī lil-fā'il), meaning: they intend to fight the polytheists in what follows and are eager for it, so its indication of the omitted part is even more evident.

﴿بِأنَّهم ظُلِمُوا﴾ means: because they were wronged. They were the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them. The polytheists would harm them, and they would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) with those who had been beaten and those whose heads had been wounded, complaining of injustice to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) would say: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight until they emigrate." Then this verse was revealed. It is the first verse revealed about fighting after the prohibition of it, in about seventy-some verses.

﴿وَإنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى نَصْرِهِمْ لَقَدِيرٌ﴾ is a promise to them of victory and a confirmation of the noble promise of defence mentioned earlier, and a declaration that its intent is not merely rescuing them from the hands of the polytheists but granting them dominance and making them victorious over them. The information about God Most High's power over their victory comes in the manner of divine majesty (kibriyā'). It is emphasized with the word of affirmation (ka-limat al-taḥqīq, i.e. inna), and the lām is for further affirmation of its content and for increasing the settling of the believers' hearts.

His Exalted saying: ﴿those who have been driven out of their homes﴾ is in the genitive position, as a qualifier (ṣifah) of the first relative pronoun (mawṣūl), or as an explanatory apposition (bayān) to it, or as a substitute (badal) for it. It may also be in the accusative position by way of praise (madḥ), or in the nominative position with an implied subject (mubtada'), the clause then being nominative by way of praise. By "their homes" is meant Makkah the Honoured.

﴿without right﴾ is related to ﴿were driven out﴾, meaning: they were driven out without anything that would necessitate their expulsion.

His Exalted saying: ﴿except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿right﴾, meaning: without any cause other than monotheism, which ought to have been a cause for acknowledgement and empowerment, not for expulsion and banishment. However, this is not in its apparent sense, but in the manner of the saying of al-Nabigha:

﴿There is no fault in them, except that their swords / have notches in them from the clashing of the battalions.﴾

It is also said that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi', i.e. not from the same category).

﴿And were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others﴾: by empowering the believers over the disbelievers in every age and time. It is also read as "difā'" (دِفاعٌ).

﴿there would have been demolished﴾: would have been ruined by the domination of the polytheists over the people of the religions. It is also read as "huddimat" (هُدِّمَتْ) with a light (unemphatic) doubling of the letter.

﴿monasteries﴾ for the monastic life, ﴿and churches﴾ for the Christians, ﴿and synagogues﴾, meaning: and houses of worship (kanā'is) for the Jews, so called because prayer (ṣalāh) is performed in them. It is also said that its origin is ṣiltā (صِلْوَتا) in Hebrew, which was then Arabized.

﴿and mosques﴾ for the Muslims, ﴿in which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾: meaning much mention, or for a long time. This is a qualifier of praise (ṣifah madḥiyyah) for the mosques, singled out for it to indicate their excellence and the excellence of their people. It is also said that it is a qualifier of all four, but this is not so, for the explanation of the mention of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the monasteries, churches and synagogues after the abrogation (naskh, i.e. the cancellation) of their legislation is something that the context does not require and that minds do not accept.

﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾: meaning, and by Allah, Allah will surely help whoever helps His friends, or whoever helps His religion. Allah, Mighty is His authority, has indeed fulfilled His promise by empowering the Emigrants and the Helpers over the chiefs of the Arabs, the Chosroes of the non-Arabs, the Caesars of the Romans, and He made them inherit their land and their homes.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful﴾ over everything He wills, among which is His helping them.

﴿Mighty﴾: nothing prevents Him and nothing repels Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 41:

﴿Those who, if We establish them firmly in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong.﴾ This is a description from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of those who were expelled from their homes, concerning the good conduct that would come from them when He established them in the land and gave them the reins of governance. It indicates a noble promise in the most eloquent and most subtle manner.

It is related from Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "By Allah, this is praise before trial." He means: Allah praised them before they had done the good that they went on to do. They said: In it is evidence for the soundness of the rule of the Rightly Guided Caliphs (al-Khulafa' al-Rashidun), because He did not grant establishment and the execution of command together with a just conduct to anyone other than them from among the Emigrants, [and] He took account of that for the Helpers and the Freed Captives (al-Tulaqa'). It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: "alladhina" is a substitute (badal) for His saying "man yansuruhu" (whoever supports Him).

﴿And to Allah belongs﴾ exclusively ﴿the outcome of all affairs﴾, for their final return is to His judgment and decree alone. In it is an affirmation of the promise of making His friends triumphant and raising His word.

(p-110) ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, and ʿAad, and Thamud had already denied [their messengers] before them.﴾ This is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), containing the generous promise of destroying those disbelievers who oppose him, and a specification of the manner of God's promised help to him, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God will surely help those who help Him﴾, and a statement that the outcome of all affairs returns to Him, Exalted is He. The use of the present tense in the conditional clause, although the denial has actually occurred, is because the purpose is to console him (ﷺ) concerning what follows from the denial of the anticipated grief; that is: "And if you grieve over their denial of you, know that you are not unique in that, for the people of Noah, ʿAad, and Thamud denied [their messengers] before the denial of your people of you."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 44:

﴿And the people of Madyan﴾. That is, their messengers, from among those who are mentioned and those who are not mentioned. It was omitted because the intended meaning is fully apparent, or because the intended meaning is the act itself, i.e., "the people of Nuh committed the denial," and so on to the end.

﴿And Musa was denied﴾. The noble arrangement has been altered by mentioning the object and building the verb on it, not because his people, the Banu Isra'il, denied him, for they did not deny him, but rather the Copts (al-Qibt) denied him. This is because that would only require that they not be mentioned under the designation of being the people of Musa, not under some other designation. Moreover, the Banu Isra'il also denied him more than once, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly﴾, and similar noble verses. Rather, it is to announce that their denial of him was in the utmost abomination, since his signs were in complete clarity.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾: that is, I granted them time until the cords of their terms were cut. The "fa" (فَ, so) is for the sequencing of the respite of each group of the deniers upon the denial of that group, not for the sequencing of the respite of all upon the denial of all. The placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun referring to the deniers is to censure them for disbelief and to explicitly name the deniers of Musa, peace be upon him, since they were not explicitly mentioned previously.

﴿Then I seized them﴾. That is, I seized each group of the deniers after the expiry of the period of their respite and reprieve.

﴿So how was My rejection?﴾. That is, My rejection of them by destruction; that is, that was at the utmost of horror and dreadfulness.

وقوله تعالى: ﴿فَكَأَيِّن مِّن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ منصوب بفعل مضمر يفسره قوله تعالى: ﴿أَهْلَكْنَاهَا﴾، أي: فأهلكنا كثيرًا من القرى بإهلاك أهلها. والجملة بدل من قوله تعالى: "فَكَيْفَ كَانَ نَكِيرِ"، أو مرفوع على الابتداء (mubtada’) وأهلكناها خبره، أي: فكثير من القرى أهلكناها. وقُرئ: "أَهْلَكْتُهَا" على وفق قوله تعالى: ﴿فَأَمْلَيْتُ لِلْكَافِرِينَ ثُمَّ أَخَذْتُهُمْ فَكَيْفَ كَانَ نَكِيرِ﴾.

﴿وَهِيَ ظَالِمَةٌ﴾ جملة حالية (hal) من مفعول "أَهْلَكْنَا". وقوله تعالى: ﴿فَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ﴾ معطوف على "أَهْلَكْنَاهَا" على "وَهِيَ ظَالِمَةٌ" لأنها حال، والإهلاك ليس في حال خوائها؛ فعلى الأول لا محل له من الإعراب (i'rab) كالمعطوف عليه، وعلى الثاني في محل الرفع لعطفه على الخبر. والخواء: إما بمعنى السقوط من خوى النجم إذا سقط، فالمعنى: فهي ساقطة حيطانها.

(p-111) ﴿عَلَى عُرُوشِهَا﴾ أي: سقوفها، بأن تعطل بنيانها فخرّت سقوفها، ثم تهدمت حيطانها فسقطت فوق السقوف. وإسناد السقوط على العروش إليها لتنزيل الحيطان منزلة كل البنيان لكونها عمدة فيه. وإما بمعنى الخلو من خوى المنزل إذا خلا من أهله، فالمعنى: فهي خالية مع بقاء عروشها وسلامتها، فتكون "على" بمعنى "مع". ويجوز أن يكون ﴿عَلَى عُرُوشِهَا﴾ خبرًا بعد خبر، أي: فهي خالية وهي على عروشها، أي: قائمة مشرفة على عروشها، على معنى أن السقوف سقطت إلى الأرض وبقيت الحيطان قائمة فهي مشرفة على السقوف الساقطة. وإسناد الإشراف إلى الكل مع كونه حال الحيطان لما مرّ آنفًا.

﴿وَبِئْرٍ مُعَطَّلَةٍ﴾ معطوف على "قَرْيَةٍ"، أي: وكم بئر عارية في البوادي تُركت لا يُستقى منها لهلاك أهلها. وقُرئ بالتخفيف من أعطله بمعنى: عطّله.

﴿وَقَصْرٍ مَّشِيدٍ﴾ مرفوع البنيان، أو مجصّص، أخليناه عن ساكنيه. وهذا يؤيد كون معنى خاوية على عروشها خالية مع بقاء عروشها. وقيل: المراد بالبئر: بئر بسفح جبل بحضرموت، وبالقصر: قصر مشرف على قلّته، كانا لقوم حنظلة بن صفوان من بقايا قوم صالح، فلما قتلوه أهلكهم الله تعالى وعطّلهما.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 46:

﴿Have they not traveled through the earth⁠﴾ is an exhortation to them to journey so that they may see the places where the destroyed peoples perished, and thereby take heed. Although they had traveled through it, since they did not travel for the sake of taking heed, they were treated as though they had not traveled, so they were urged to do so. The fa' (fa, "so/then") here conjoins what follows it to an implied element required by the context, i.e., "They were heedless, so they did not travel through it."

﴿so that they would have⁠﴾ hearts with which they understand, by means of what they witnessed of the material of lessons and the loci of insight, ﴿hearts with which they understand⁠﴾ what must be understood of monotheism (tawhid, the oneness of God), ﴿or ears with which they hear⁠﴾ what must be heard of revelation, or of the reports of the destroyed nations from those among the people who neighbor them, for they know their circumstances better than others do.

﴿Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded⁠﴾: the pronoun (inna, "indeed") refers to the matter (al-qissa, the story), or it is an ambiguous pronoun explained by "the eyes" (al-absar) that follows. In "taʿma" (is blinded) there is a pronoun referring to it, and the apparent noun has been placed in its stead.

﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded⁠﴾: that is, the defect does not lie in their sense perceptions, but in their intellects, through following desire and immersion in heedlessness. The mention of "the breasts" serves to emphasize and to negate the supposition of figurative usage. It also draws attention to the fact that real blindness is not the commonly understood kind, which is specific to sight. It is said: "When the verse ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter⁠﴾ was revealed, Ibn Umm Maktum said: 'O Messenger of God, I am blind in this world; shall I be blind in the Hereafter?' Then this verse was revealed."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 47:**

﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. They were utterly denying the coming of the threatened punishment. They were only asking for it to hasten as mockery of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and as a challenge to him according to their own claim. So He related this of them in a manner of rebuke and disapproval. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God will not fail His promise﴾, is either a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), brought to show the falsehood of their denial of its coming within their asking for it hastily and to demonstrate their error in this. It is as if it were said: how do they deny the coming of the promised punishment when He, exalted is He, never fails His promise, and the promise has already preceded, so it must come inevitably? Or it is a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tiradiyya*) explaining what has been mentioned.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾, is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustani'fa*) if the first was circumstantial, and is coordinated with it (*ma'tufa 'alayha*) if the first was parenthetical. It is brought to show their error in the aforementioned hastening, by demonstrating the complete breadth of the expanse of His forbearance and dignity, and to show the extreme narrowness of their own reckoning. This implies that a short period is, in His presence, lengthy periods for them, as His saying, exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿Indeed, they see it as distant﴾ ﴿but We see it as near﴾. For this reason they regard its coming as distant, take it as a pretext for denying it, and presume to hasten it, not realizing that the standard by which all matters are measured, both in their occurrence and in their report, is what is with Him, exalted is He, in terms of measure.

The recitation *yu'iddūna* ("they count") in the third person is more suitable to this meaning, meaning that the hasteners count it. In the well-known recitation, the address is also directed to them, by way of *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person). However, the apparent sense is that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and those believers with him. It has been said that what is meant by His promise, exalted is He, is the fixed appointed time (*ajal musamma*) set for the destruction of every nation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, and were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾. In that case the first clause, whether circumstantial or parenthetical, shows the falsehood of hastening it by showing the impossibility of its coming before its appointed time, and the final clause shows its falsehood by showing that it is based on the prolonging of what is short in His presence, in the manner already explained. Then there is in the noble text, in that case, no reference to their denial, which they concealed beneath the hastening. Rather, the answer is based on the apparent content of their speech, and refuting their denial is sufficient by mentioning the fate of those before them who were like them.

Taking what is hastened to be the punishment of the Hereafter, and taking "day" as an expression for the day of punishment, prolonged because of its severity, or for the long days of the Hereafter in their literal sense, or prolonged because of the severity of its punishment, is not supported by the sequence or context of the sublime text. Each of these clearly indicates that what is meant is the worldly punishment, and that the extended time is that which passed over them before its arrival, by way of respite and delay, not the time coinciding with it.

Is it not seen (as relevant) that his saying, exalted is He, ﴿And how many a town﴾ and so on, is, as was previously stated from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them﴾, clear that what is meant is the swift, severe seizing after extended respite? That is, "and how many a people of a town," where the modifier (al-mudaf) is elided and the modified (al-mudaf ilayhi) takes its place in i'rab (grammatical case and syntactic analysis), and the pronouns and rulings are made to refer back to the people, for the sake of hyperbole in generality and in striking awe.

﴿I gave her respite﴾, just as I gave respite to these people, until they denied the coming of the punishment they had been promised and hastened it, mocking their messengers, as these people did.

﴿And she was wrongdoing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), conveying the perfection of His forbearance, exalted is He, and indirectly hinting at the wrongdoing of those who hasten (the punishment). That is: I gave her respite while she was in the state of wrongdoing, deserving the hastening of punishment, like the practice of these people.

﴿Then I seized her﴾ with punishment and chastisement after the long extension of respite and delay.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Me is the destination﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tirad tadhyili), confirming what precedes it and explicitly stating what that indirectly conveyed, namely that the outcome of the affair of those who hasten is also the severe seizing mentioned. That is: the return of all of them is to My judgment, not to anyone other than Me, neither independently nor as a partner. So I will do with them what I do, that which befits their deeds.

Say, "O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you." I warn you with a clear warning, by what has been revealed to me of the reports of the destroying nations, without my having any part in bringing about the punishment you are promised, so that you hasten me to it. The restriction to warning, together with the statement of the condition of the two groups after it, is because, as has been indicated, the context of the discourse concerns the polytheists and their punishment. The believers and their reward are mentioned only as an increase in their rage.

(p-113) ﴿So those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them there is forgiveness﴾ for whatever sins slipped from them, ﴿and a generous provision﴾, which is Paradise. The "generous" (karim) of every kind is that which combines its excellences and attains its perfections.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 51:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾: that is, those who are "outstrippers" or "competitors" in their own assumption and estimation, hoping that their scheming against Islam will be completed for them. Its origin is from "ʿājazahu" and "ʿajjazahu" and "aʿjazahu": when one competes with another and outstrips him, because each of the two competitors wants to make the other unable to catch up with him. It has also been read as "muʿajjizīn" (ﷺ), meaning: discouraging people from faith, in which case it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah).

﴿Those﴾: the ones described with what has been mentioned of striving and frustrating [the signs] ﴿are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾: that is, those who constantly abide in the kindled Fire. It has also been said that "al-Jaḥīm" is the name of one of its levels (darakāt).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 52:**

﴿Never did We send before you any messenger (rasul) or prophet (nabi)﴾. The *rasul* is one whom God Most High sends with a new law (shari'ah), calling people to it. The *nabi* is more general: it includes the one sent to affirm an earlier law, such as the prophets of the Children of Israel who came between Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) likened the scholars of his community to them. Thus the *nabi* is more general than the *rasul*. This is indicated by the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the prophets and said: "They are one hundred and twenty-four thousand." It was said: "How many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and thirteen, a great throng."

It was also said: the *rasul* is one who, in addition to a miracle, is given a book revealed to him, while the *nabi* who is not a *rasul* has no book. It was also said: the *rasul* is one to whom the angel comes with revelation, while the *nabi* is a term applied to him and to one to whom revelation comes in a dream.

﴿except when he wished﴾, that is, he prepared in his soul what he desired. ﴿Satan cast into his wish﴾, into his longing, that which would cause him to be occupied with the world, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, my heart is veiled, so I seek forgiveness from God seventy times a day."

﴿Then God abrogates what Satan casts﴾, that is, He nullifies it and removes it, by His protection (*'ismah*) of him from inclining towards it, and by guiding him to what dispels it.

﴿Then God establishes His verses﴾, that is, He confirms His verses which call to total absorption in the affairs of the Truth. The use of the present tense in both verbs indicates continuous renewal, and the explicit mention of the Divine Name (Allah) in the place of a pronoun serves to increase the affirmation and to indicate that divinity (*uluhiyyah*) necessitates the rulings of His dazzling verses.

﴿And God is All-Knowing﴾, exceedingly knowing of everything that is capable of being known, including what proceeds from the servants of words and deeds, whether intentionally or by error.

﴿All-Wise﴾ in everything He does. The explicit mention here also serves the same purpose as above, along with what it contains of emphasis on the independence of the concluding interjection (*al-i'tiraḍ al-tadhyili*).

It was said: he (the Prophet) spoke to himself about the removal of his poverty, and so this was revealed. It was also said: out of his eagerness for the faith of his people, he wished that there would descend upon him that which would bring them close to him, and this desire continued with him until he was in their assembly, and the sura of al-Najm was revealed to him. He began to recite it, and when he reached "And Manat, the third, the other," Satan whispered to him until his tongue slipped, unintentionally, into saying: "Those are the exalted *gharaniq* (cranes), and indeed their intercession is to be hoped for." The polytheists rejoiced at this until they joined him in prostration when he prostrated at its end, so that no believer or polytheist remained in the mosque except that he prostrated. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, alerted him, and he hastened to correct it. God, Mighty and Majestic, consoled him with this verse. But this is rejected by the verifying scholars (*al-muhaqqiqin*), and even if it is authentic, it is a trial by which the one firm in faith is distinguished from the one who wavers in it.

It was also said: (p-114) *tamanna* here means "recited," as in his saying:

*"He recited the Book of God on the first night, as David recited the Psalms among the messengers."*

And his *umniyyah* (wish) is his recitation. The casting of Satan into it is that he spoke these words raising his voice, such that the listeners thought it was from the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ). This has been rejected on the grounds that it too undermines trust in the Qur'an, and it is not resolved by God's saying: ﴿Then God abrogates what Satan casts, then God establishes His verses﴾, because this too admits of that interpretation. The verse also indicates the permissibility of forgetfulness (*sahw*) on the part of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the occurrence of whispering (*waswasah*) to them.

﴿لِيَجْعَلَ ما يُلْقِي الشَّيْطانُ﴾ is a purpose clause (*ʿillah*, reason or purpose) for what is indicated by the preceding mention of Satan's casting, namely that God, exalted is He, enabled Satan to do this with respect to the Prophet ﷺ specifically, as the context of the noble discourse (*naẓm*) indicates. This is because His enabling of casting with respect to the other prophets, peace be upon them, cannot be explained by what follows. In it is also an indication that what Satan casts is a manifest matter, which both the one upholding the truth (*al-muḥiqq*) and the one upholding falsehood (*al-mubṭil*) recognise.

﴿فِتْنَةً لِلَّذِينَ في قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ﴾ means: doubt and hypocrisy, as in His saying: ﴿in their hearts is a disease ...﴾ the verse.

﴿والقاسِيَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ means: the polytheists. ﴿وَإنَّ الظّالِمِينَ﴾ means: the two groups mentioned. Placing the explicit noun in the place of their pronoun is to record upon them the attribute of wrongdoing, along with what they were described with of disease and hardness.

﴿لَفِي شِقاقٍ بَعِيدٍ﴾ means: intense enmity and complete opposition. Describing the schism (*shiqāq*) as "far" (*baʿīd*), although the thing characterised by it is in reality the schism itself, is for the sake of emphasis (*mubālaghah*). The clause is a concluding parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī*) that confirms the content of what precedes it.

And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it (i.e., the Qur'an) is the truth from your Lord. It is said: "That they may know that the empowerment of Satan to cast (the suggestion) is the truth, containing a profound wisdom and a beautiful end, because it is among what has been his (Allah's) customary practice among the human species since Adam, peace be upon him. Then there is no need to restrict the empowerment in what preceded to the casting in regard to him, peace be upon him. But his saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that they may believe in it﴾, i.e., in the Qur'an, that is, that they may remain steadfast in faith in it or increase in faith by rejecting what Satan casts, so that their hearts ﴿humble themselves﴾ to it through submission, fear, and compliance with what it contains of commands and prohibitions, rebuts this. And returning the two pronouns, especially the second, to the empowerment of Satan to cast is something that has no basis.

﴿And indeed, Allah is the guide of those who believe﴾, i.e., in religious matters, especially in the slippery places and difficulties of which this is one.

﴿to a straight path﴾, which is the sound reasoning that leads to the clear truth. The sentence is an interjection confirming what came before it.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on surah 22, verse 55:

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it﴾, that is, in doubt and dispute, ﴿about it﴾, that is, about the Qur'an. It was also said that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ). The first view is the more apparent, as shown by what precedes it in His words, ﴿then Allah abolishes what Satan throws in, then Allah establishes His verses﴾, and His words, ﴿that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they may believe in it﴾, and what follows it in His words, ﴿and they denied Our signs﴾. As for permitting the pronoun to refer to "what Satan threw into his wish" (p-115), this has no justification, because that is not among their defects that continue until the stated term. Rather, their doubt concerns the Qur'an itself. Nor does it help to take *min* (مِن) as causal (*sababiyya*) rather than inceptive (*ibtida'iyya*, indicating origin), because their continuous doubt is, just as it did not originate from that, not "emanating from it" (*mashi'a* ماشِئَةً, i.e., arising from it), for it is necessarily continuous among them from the time the noble Qur'an was revealed.

﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾, that is, the Resurrection itself, as His words indicate, ﴿suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, for it is the Hour that is described as coming in this manner, not its portents. It was also said that it refers to death.

﴿or there comes upon them the punishment of a barren day﴾, that is, a day after which there is no day, as if every day gives birth to the days after it, so the day after which there is no day is barren (*'aqim* عَقِيمًا). What is meant by it is also the Hour, as if it were said, "or its punishment comes upon them," and the pronoun was replaced by this phrase for greater awe. There is no way to take the Hour as referring to its portents, for the reason you have understood. As for what has been said, that the meaning is a day of war in which they kill one another, like the Day of Badr, and that it was so named because the children of women are killed in it, so they become as if they were women who have not borne children (*'uqum* عُقُمٌ); or because the combatants are "sons of war," and when they are killed she becomes barren, i.e., bereaved (*thakla* ثَكْلى), so the day is described by her attribute in a broadened sense; or because there is no good for them in it, from which comes "the barren wind" (*al-rih al-'aqim* الرِّيحُ العَقِيمُ), which brings no rain and does not fertilize trees; or because it has no equal, since the angels fight in it, peace be upon them: all of this is not supported at all by the context of the noble composition. How could it be, when the restriction of sovereignty and complete disposal in it to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and then the explanation of what judgment of His, exalted is He, takes place in it between the two groups, with reward and punishment in the Hereafter, requires that its meaning is the Day of Resurrection, a clear judgment without doubt.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 56:**

﴿The sovereignty﴾: that is, the overpowering authority, complete control, and disposal without any restriction.

﴿On that Day belongs to Allah﴾ alone, with no partner at all, such that no one has any disposal in any matter, whether real or metaphorical, formal or substantive, as there is in this world. In this world some have a formal disposal to a certain extent. The *tanwin* (nunation, *al-tanwin*) is not a substitute for what the terminal point indicates, namely the removal of their doubt (*maryatihim*), as has been said, nor for what that entails, namely their faith, as has been said. This is because the qualifying condition attached to "the Day," since it is placed between the two parts of the sentence, must be the pivot of its ruling, that is, that sovereignty belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and what follows from it of reward and punishment. There is no doubt that their faith or the removal of their doubt has no connection whatsoever with what has been mentioned, let alone being its pivot. Therefore there is no way to take either of them as conditioned by "the Day," definitively. What the mentioned matter actually turns upon is the coming of the Hour, which is the end of the disposals of creation and the beginning of the manifestation of the rulings of the True King, may His majesty be exalted. Thus *tanwin* is a substitute for the very sentence that serves as the terminal point of their doubt. The meaning is: sovereignty on the Day when the Hour, or its punishment, comes upon them, belongs to Allah, the Exalted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will judge between them﴾ is a resumptive sentence that comes as an answer to a question arising from the statement that sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah. As if it were said: "What will be done with them then?" So it was said: He will judge between the group of those who believed in it and those who disputed about it, by way of recompense.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So as for those who believed﴾, etc., is an explanation and detailing of the stated ruling. That is: those who believed in the Noble Qur'an and did not dispute about it, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ in compliance with what they were commanded within it, ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾; that is, they will abide therein.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 57:

﴿And as for those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾, i.e., they persist in that and continue in it. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative pointing back to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), with regard to its being characterized by what is in the scope of the relative clause (al-silah) of disbelief and denial. The sense of distance in it serves to signal the remoteness of their rank in evil and corruption (p-116). That is: those who are described by what has been mentioned of disbelief and denial. It is the subject (mubtada'). The words of the Exalted, ﴿for them is a punishment﴾, form a nominal clause consisting of a subject and a predicate placed before it, and it occurs as the predicate (khabar) of ﴿those﴾. Alternatively, ﴿for them﴾ is the predicate of ﴿those﴾, and ﴿a punishment﴾ is raised as the agent (fa'iliyyah) by the stability (al-istiqrar) within the prepositional phrase, because it relies on the subject. ﴿Those﴾ together with its predicate, on both views, is the predicate of the relative pronoun. Introducing it with the particle fa' (so) indicates that the punishment of the disbelievers is due to their evil deeds, just as the stripping of the first relative clause's predicate of such a connection signals that the reward of the believers is by way of grace, not because good deeds necessitate it.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿humiliating﴾, are an attribute of ﴿punishment﴾, emphasizing what the indefiniteness (tanwin) conveys of magnitude. In it there is intensification in many respects, which is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 58:

﴿Those who emigrated in the way of Allah﴾ That is, in jihad, as is hinted at by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿then they are slain or they die﴾, that is, in the course of emigration. The place of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is nominative, as the subject of the sentence (mubtada').

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah will surely provide for them﴾ are the answer to an implied oath (qasam mahdhuf), and the clause is its predicate. Whoever prevents an oath-clause and its answer from being the predicate of the subject holds that there is an implied verb of saying (yudmiru qawlan) which is the predicate, and the clause is quoted by it. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿a goodly provision﴾ are either a second object (maf'ul thani), on the basis that it is of the type of "al-ra'y and al-dhabh" (the construction in which the verb governs two objects), meaning "one provided with a goodly provision", or an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), and what is meant by it is the bounty of Paradise that never ends. He equated the two in the promise only because they are equal in purpose; and the principle is that the degrees of goodness vary, so the condition of those provided for may vary according to the variation of goodly provisions. It is narrated that some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Prophet of Allah, these who were slain in the way of Allah, we know what good Allah has given them, and we strive along with you as they strove; so what will be for us if we die with you?" Then it was revealed. It is also said: it was revealed concerning groups who went out from Makkah to Madinah for the hijrah, and the polytheists followed them and killed them.

﴿And indeed Allah is surely the best of providers﴾, for He provides without reckoning, along with the fact that what He provides no one other than Him is able to provide. The clause is a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiradh tadhyili) confirming what precedes it.

The phrase ﴿لَيُدْخِلَنَّهم مُدْخَلا يَرْضَوْنَهُ﴾ ("He will surely admit them to an entrance they will be pleased with") is either a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿لَيَرْزُقَنَّهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("God will surely provide for them"), or a resumptive new clause (isti'naf) confirming what that statement contains. The word "mudkhalan" (entrance) is either a noun of place, meaning Paradise, in which case it is the second object of the verb "to admit" (al-idkhal), or a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi) used to emphasize its verb.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: The reason it is said "they will be pleased with it" is that they will see in it what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to the heart of any human being, so they will be pleased with it.

﴿وَإنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is surely All-Knowing") of their circumstances and the circumstances of their adversaries, ﴿حَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Most Forbearing") who does not hasten to punish them.

ذَلِكَ (dhalika, "that"): خَبَرُ مُبْتَدَأٍ مَحْذُوفٍ، أيِ: الأمْرُ ذَلِكَ
The predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the matter is that.

Translation: "That" is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: the matter is that. The sentence serves to confirm what precedes it and to alert that what follows is a new, independent statement.

﴿وَمَن عاقَبَ بِمِثْلِ ما عُوقِبَ بِهِ﴾ أيْ: لَمْ يَزِدْ في الِاقْتِصاصِ، وإنَّما سُمِّيَ الِابْتِداءُ بِالعِقابِ الَّذِي هو جَزاءُ الجِنايَةِ لِلْمُشاكَلَةِ أوْ لِكَوْنِهِ سَبَبًا لَهُ ﴿ثُمَّ بُغِيَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ بِالمُعاوَدَةِ إلى العُقُوبَةِ ﴿لَيَنْصُرَنَّهُ اللَّهُ﴾ عَلى مَن بَغى عَلَيْهِ لا مَحالَةَ ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ أيْ: مُبالَغٌ في العَفْوِ والغُفْرانِ، (p-117)فَيَعْفُو عَنِ المُنْتَصِرِ ويَغْفِرُ لَهُ ما صَدَرَ عَنْهُ مِن تَرْجِيحِ الِانْتِقامِ عَلى العَفْوِ والصَّبْرِ المَندُوبِ إلَيْهِما بِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وَلَمَن صَبَرَ وغَفَرَ إنَّ ذَلِكَ ...﴾ أيْ: ما ذُكِرَ مِنَ الصَّبْرِ والمَغْفِرَةِ لَمِن عَزْمِ الأُمُورِ، فَإنَّ فِيهِ حَثًّا بَلِيغًا عَلى العَفْوِ والمَغْفِرَةِ فَإنَّهُ تَعالى مَعَ كَمالِ قدرته لَمّا كانَ يَعْفُو ويَغْفِرُ فَغَيْرُهُ أوْلى بِذَلِكَ، وتَنْبِيهًا عَلى أنَّهُ تَعالى قادِرٌ عَلى العُقُوبَةِ إذْ لا يُوصَفُ بِالعَفْوِ إلّا القادِرُ عَلى ضِدِّهِ.

Translation:

﴿That [is so]. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, then he is wronged again, Allah will surely help him.﴾ That is, he does not exceed in retribution. The initiation of punishment, which is the requital of the offence, is called by that name either for the sake of verbal parallelism (al-musha-kalah) or because it is a cause of it. ﴿Then he is wronged again﴾ by returning to punishment. ﴿Allah will surely help him﴾ against the one who wronged him, without doubt. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Most Pardoning, Most Forgiving﴾ — that is, exceedingly abundant in pardon and forgiveness, (p-117) so He pardons the one who seeks redress and forgives him what proceeded from him of preferring retaliation over pardon and patience, both of which are recommended by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination...﴾ That is, what has been mentioned of patience and forgiveness is among the firm resolutions of affairs, for in it there is an emphatic exhortation to pardon and forgiveness. For He, Exalted is He, despite His perfect power, pardons and forgives, so others are more deserving of that. It also serves as an alert that He, Exalted is He, is capable of punishment, since only one who is capable of the opposite is described as Pardoning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 61:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the victory, and the sense of distance in it is to signal the elevated rank of that victory. Its position is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, meaning: due to the fact that it is part of His Exalted affairs and His customary way (sunan) to make some of His creatures prevail over others, and to alternate between opposing things. He expressed this by the entering of one of the two alternating phases into the other, either by adding to one what is lost from the other, or by bringing one of them into the place of the other, because it is the most manifest and clearest of matters.

﴿And that Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of all things heard, among which is the speech of the one who retaliates.

﴿All-Seeing﴾ of all things seen, among which are His actions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 62:

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ i.e., the attribute of having the perfection of power and knowledge that was mentioned, and what it contains of the sense of distance because of what passed just before. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿bi-anna Allaha huwa al-haqq﴾ [because God is the Truth], the One who is necessary in His essence, established in His self, attributes and acts, alone. For the necessity of His existence and His oneness require that He is the origin of everything that exists among existing things, knowing all that is known. Or [the meaning is]: the one established in divinity, so none is fit for it except one who is knowing and powerful.

﴿wa-anna ma yad'una min dunihi﴾ [and that what they call upon besides Him] as a god. It is also read in the passive form (ببناء للمفعول), with the waw being for ما (لِما), since it refers to the false gods. It is also read with the ta' (بِالتّاءِ), addressing the polytheists.

﴿huwa al-batil﴾ [it is the false], i.e., that which is non-existent in itself, or the false is their divinity.

﴿wa-anna Allaha huwa al-'Aliyyu﴾ [and that God is the Most High] over all things, ﴿al-Kabir﴾ [the Great], far above having any associate, there being nothing higher than Him in rank or greater in dominion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 63:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky?﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir), as is made clear by the nominative case in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and the earth becomes green﴾, being conjoined by coordination (al-'atf) to "anzala" (sent down). The choice of the present-tense form (sigha al-istiqbal) serves either to indicate the renewal and continuity of the effect of the sending down, or to bring to mind the image of the greening.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle (latif)﴾, whose subtlety or knowledge reaches everything that is vast and everything that is fine, ﴿Acquainted (khabir)﴾ with what befits of wise arrangements, outwardly and inwardly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 64:

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ by creation, dominion, and disposal; ﴿and indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghaniyy), the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾ — free of need from everything, the One deserving of praise for His attributes and His actions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 65:

﴿Do you not see that God has subjected to you whatever is on the earth﴾ That is: He made the things in it tractable and prepared for your benefits, so that you may dispose of them as you wish, nothing being harder than stone, stronger than iron, or more awe-inspiring than fire, yet all of them are subjected to you. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the direct object, as has been mentioned many times before, serves to give emphasis to the fronted element, to hasten the joy and to build anticipation for what is delayed.

﴿And the ship﴾ is coordinated with "mā" or with the noun of "inna". It is also read in the nominative, on the basis of it being the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

﴿running on the sea by His command﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the ship" according to the first reading, and a predicate (khabar) according to the last two.

﴿And He withholds the sky from falling upon the earth﴾ That is: from falling, or out of aversion to its falling, by having created it in a form inclined to remain held up.

﴿except by His permission﴾ That is: by His will, and that will be on the Day of Resurrection. In this there is a refutation of the view that its being held up is by its own essence, since it is equal in corporeality to all other bodies which are receptive to the downward inclination, and so it accepts it as the others do.

﴿Indeed God is, toward the people, Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ in that He prepared for them the means of their livelihood, opened for them the doors of benefits, and made clear to them the methods of reasoning from the signs both of creation and of revelation.

And it is He who gave you life, after you were lifeless matter, elements and sperm-drops, as was detailed at the beginning of this noble surah.

Then He causes you to die when your terms arrive, then He gives you life again at the Resurrection. Indeed, man is ungrateful: that is, one who denies the blessings despite their being evident. This is a description of the species by way of describing some of its individuals.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 67:

﴿For every community﴾ is a resumed statement, brought to rebuke his contemporaries ﷺ among the People of the Scriptures (ahl al-adyan al-samawiyya) from disputing with him ﷺ, by describing the state of the laws they hold fast to and by showing their error in consideration. That is: for every specific community among the past and remaining communities ﴿We have made﴾, i.e., We have established and designated, ﴿a rite (mansak)﴾, i.e., a particular law, not for another community among them, meaning: We have designated each law for a specific community among the communities, such that no community among them oversteps its designated law to another law, neither independently nor jointly.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they are its performers (nasikuhu)﴾ is a descriptive clause for "mansak," emphasizing the restriction (qasr) derived from placing the prepositional phrase before the verb. The pronoun [in "they are its performers"] refers to ﴿every community﴾ in terms of its members, meaning: that specific community are its performers and those who act by it, not another community. So the community that existed from the time of Musa, peace be upon him, until the time of Isa, peace be upon him, had the Torah as its rite; they are its performers and those who act by it, and no others. And the community that existed from the time of Isa until the time of the Prophet ﷺ had the Gospel as its rite; they are its performers and those who act by it, and no others. As for the community present at the time of the Prophet ﷺ and those after them among the people existing until the Day of Resurrection, they are one community whose rite is the Furqan alone, as has passed in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so let them not dispute with you in the matter﴾ is for a divine consequence or what necessitates it upon what precedes it, for His designating for each community of the communities, of which this community is among them, a law independent such that no community among them oversteps its designated law, necessitates the obedience of these people to the Messenger of God ﷺ and their not disputing with him in matters of religion, on their claim that their law is what was designated for their first forefathers from the Torah and the Gospel; for these two are laws for those who passed among the communities before their abrogation (intisakh), and these people are an independent community whose rite is the Glorious Qur'an alone. The prohibition is either on its literal sense, or its generality is a prohibition to him ﷺ from paying attention to their dispute with the Prophet on their stated claim. As for making it an expression of a prohibition to him ﷺ (p-119) from disputing with them, the context does not support it. It has been read as "fa-la yanza'annaka" (so let them not turn you away), as an incitement of him ﷺ and an emphasis on his steadfastness. In any case, the object of the dispute is what we have mentioned, and restricting it to the matter of the rites (nasa'ik) and making it an expression of the saying of the Khuza'iyyin and others to the Muslims, "What is with you that you eat what you have killed and do not eat what God has killed," which has no basis whatsoever, how could it not be so, since it would require that eating carrion and all the falsehoods they adhere to be among the rites which God, exalted is He, has made for some communities, and no sane person doubts its invalidity.

﴿And call﴾, i.e., and call them, or call the people altogether, on the basis that they are included among them by primary inclusion, ﴿to your Lord﴾: to His unification and worship, as was made clear to them in their rite and their law.

﴿Indeed you are surely upon a straight guidance﴾, i.e., a path leading to the truth, upright. What is meant by it is either the religion and the law, or their proofs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 68:

﴿And if they dispute with you﴾ after the truth has become manifest, by what has been mentioned of verification and the binding of proof upon them, ﴿then say﴾ to them, by way of warning, ﴿Allah knows best what you do﴾ of falsehoods, of which disputation is among the sum.

Allah will judge between you (﴿Allah yahkumu baynakum﴾) — He will separate the believers among you from the disbelievers (يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ مِنكم والكافِرِينَ) ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ) by reward and punishment, just as He made the separation in this world by proofs and signs (بِالحُجَجِ والآياتِ).

﴿Concerning that about which you used to differ﴾ (﴿فِيما كُنْتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ﴾) — concerning matters of religion (مِن أمْرِ الدِّينِ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 70:

﴿Did you not know﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) confirming the content of what precedes it. The interrogative is for confirmation (taqrir), meaning: you have indeed known ﴿that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, so nothing among things is hidden from Him, and among those things is what the disbelievers say and what they do.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, i.e., what is in the heavens and the earth, ﴿is in a Book﴾, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), in which it was written before it came into being. So their affair should not trouble you, given that We know it and have it preserved.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned of knowledge and comprehensive awareness of it, and its recording in the Tablet, or the judgment between you, ﴿is easy for Allah﴾. For His knowledge and power are required by His essence, so nothing is hidden from Him, and no matter that is within His power is difficult for Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 71:

﴿And they worship besides Allah﴾ is a narration of some of the falsehoods of the polytheists and their conditions, which indicate the complete flimsiness of their intellects and the feebleness of their opinions, in that they built the matter of their religion on a foundation that has no basis in any transmitted (sam'i) or rational (aqli) proof, and in their turning away from the clear authority (sultan bayyin), which is the basis and foundation of religion, with the utmost aversion. That is, they worship, going beyond the worship of Allah.

﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾, i.e., no warrant for the permissibility of worshipping it, ﴿authority﴾, i.e., proof.

﴿and of which they have no knowledge﴾, i.e., no knowledge of the permissibility of worshipping it, derived from necessity of reason (darurat al-'aql) or from its reasoning (istidlal).

﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who committed such a great wrong, which by the self-evident judgment of intellects demands its falsehood and that it is wrong, ﴿there is no helper﴾ who would assist them by supporting their doctrine and confirming their opinion, or by averting the punishment that befalls them because of their wrongdoing.

(p-120) ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "yaʿbudūna" (they worship), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). The present tense of the verb indicates continuous, repeated recurrence.

﴿Clear﴾ means: in a state of being plainly evident in indicating the true beliefs and the truthful rulings, or in indicating the falsity of their worship of idols, or in indicating that they are from God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿You recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the munkar﴾: that is, the denial (al-inkār), like "al-mukram" in the sense of honor (al-ikrām); or the hideous, from scowling and frowning (al-tajahhum wa-al-busūr); or the evil they intend, shown by the signs of its manifestations in their conditions and appearances. The last is the most fitting to His words: ﴿they almost assault those who recite Our verses to them﴾, that is, they pounce upon them and lash out at them out of excessive rage and anger, over falsehoods they took up by blind imitation (taqlīdan). Is there any ignorance greater and more grievous than worshipping what gives no semblance of validity to its worship at all, rather what both reason and transmitted proof judge to be false, and displaying such a hideous denial toward the one who guides them to the manifest truth with clear authority? Nay. For this reason, "those who disbelieve" was placed in the position of the pronoun.

﴿Say﴾: as a rebuttal to them and a discouragement from what they intend of harming the Muslims. ﴿Shall I inform you﴾, that is, shall I address you and tell you ﴿of something worse than that﴾ which is in you: your rage at the reciters and your assault upon them; or what you intend for them of mischief; or the distress that has afflicted you because of what they recited to you.

﴿The Fire﴾: that is, it is the Fire, on the reading that this is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What is it?" It is also said that it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is His words: ﴿God has promised it to those who disbelieve﴾. It is read as "al-nāra" in the accusative by specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), and in the genitive as an apposition (badal) to "sharr" (worse). In that case the verbal clause is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), as in the first reading, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "al-nār" with "qad" implied.

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: the Fire.

O mankind, a parable has been coined, so listen to it. Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 22, verse 73:

﴿O mankind, a parable has been coined﴾, i.e., a strange state or a wondrous, marvelous story has been set forth for you, truly deserving to be called a parable (mathal) and to travel through the lands and the ages. Or it means: a parable has been made for God, i.e., a parable concerning the deserving of worship, and what is intended by this is what has been related about their worship of idols.

﴿So listen to it﴾, i.e., listen to the parable itself with reflection and contemplation, or: listen for its sake to what I say. Then His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides God﴾, etc., are an explanation of the parable and an elucidation of it according to the first reading, and a justification for the invalidity of their making the idols equal to God, may He be glorified, in the deserving of worship according to the second reading. It was also read with the yā' of the third person, both in the active and passive voice, and the returning pronoun referring to the relative clause (al-mawsul) is elided according to the first two readings.

﴿Will never create a fly﴾, i.e., they will never be able to create it, ever, despite its smallness and insignificance, for "lan" with what it carries of emphasis in negation indicates the incompatibility between the negated and that of which it is negated.

﴿Even if they gathered together for it﴾, i.e., for its creation. The answer to "law" (even if) is elided because what precedes it indicates it. The clause is coordinated with another conditional clause that is elided, relying on this one to indicate it, i.e., "if they did not gather together for it, they would never create it, and even if they gathered together for it, they would never create it," as its verification has been explained repeatedly. Both are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as if it were said: they will never create a fly (9) in any state.

﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them something﴾ is an explanation of their inability to prevent what the fly does to them after the explanation of their inability to create it, i.e., if the fly takes something from them, ﴿they would not be able to rescue it from it﴾, despite its utmost weakness. They have been made utterly ignorant in their association of others with God, the One capable of all things, the sole originator of all existing beings, by taking as images things that are the most incapable of all things. He explained this by saying that they cannot even against the least and most contemptible of living creatures, even if they united for it, but rather they cannot withstand this least and most contemptible creature, and are unable to ward it off from themselves or rescue what it snatches from them. It was said: they used to perfume them with scent and honey and shut the doors upon them, and the fly would enter through the openings and eat it.

﴿Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾, i.e., the idol-worshipper and his deity, or the fly, the seeker of what it snatches from the idol of perfume, and the idol is the one sought from it; or the idol and the fly, as if the idol were seeking it so that it might rescue from it what it snatches. Had you examined it closely, you would find the idol weaker than the fly by degrees, and its worshipper more ignorant than every ignorant person and more astray than every astray one.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 74:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure.﴾ That is: they did not know Him with His true knowledge, in that they associated partners with Him and named by His name things that are the furthest of all things from Him in fitting relation.

﴿Indeed God is All-Powerful﴾ over the creation of all possible beings and the annihilation of all existing things to the last of them.

﴿All-Mighty﴾: Overpowering over all things. You have known the condition of their gods, which are subdued; the weakest of them would humiliate the feeblest of them. The sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, namely the negation of their knowledge of Him, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 75:

﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind.﴾ [The angels] who act as intermediaries between Him, exalted is He, and the prophets, upon them be peace, through revelation.

﴿And from among mankind﴾: they are the ones singled out for pure souls, strengthened with holy power, connected to both the spiritual and the corporeal worlds. They receive from one side and convey to the other side, and their attachment to the interests of creation does not prevent them from devoting themselves to the threshold of the Truth. So they call people to Him, exalted is He, with what has been revealed to them, and they teach them His laws and rulings. It is as if He, exalted is He, when He established His oneness in divinity and denied that anything among existing things could share in it, made clear that He has servants chosen for the message, through whose response and emulation one may be drawn to His worship, mighty and majestic is He. This is the highest rank and the utmost goal for all other beings, affirming prophethood and refuting their statement: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ and their statement: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ and their saying: the angels are the daughters of Allah, and other falsehoods.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾: knowing all things heard and seen, so nothing of words and deeds is hidden from Him.
Verse 76 of Surah al-Hajj: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah are all matters returned﴾, not to anyone other than Him, neither in partnership nor independently.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 77:

﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate⁠﴾ That is: in your prayers. He commanded them with these two because they had not been performing them at the beginning of Islam, or they were [such that] they had reached [a point of performing them]. He expressed prayer (salah) by these two because they are the greatest of its pillars (arkan). Or [it means]: humble yourselves before Allah, the Exalted, and fall down to Him in prostration.

(p-122)﴿And worship your Lord⁠﴾ with all that He has made you worship Him with, ﴿and do good⁠﴾ and seek out what is best and most upright in everything you do and everything you refrain from, such as voluntary acts of obedience (nawafil al-ta'at), maintaining ties of kinship (silat al-arham), and noble character (makarim al-akhlaq).

﴿That you may succeed⁠﴾ That is: do all of these while hoping by them for success (falah), not being certain of it and not relying with confidence on your own deeds. The verse is a verse of prostration according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, due to the apparent command to prostrate in it and due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Surah al-Hajj has been favored with two prostrations; whoever does not prostrate for them, let him not recite it."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 22, verse 78:

﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him⟩. That is: for Allah, the Exalted, and for His sake, against the enemies of His religion, the apparent ones such as the people of deviation, and the hidden ones such as desire (hawa) and the self (nafs). "And from him (ﷺ) it is reported that he returned from the expedition of Tabuk and said: 'We have returned from the lesser striving (jihad) to the greater striving.'"

﴿with the striving due to Him⟩. That is: striving in which there is sincere truth for His sake alone. The word "truth" (haqq) is placed in the reverse order and attached to "striving" for emphasis, as in your saying: "He is a truly knowing scholar." The striving is attached to the pronoun as an expansion (ittisa'an), or because it is specific to Him, the Exalted, in that it is done for His sake and for His purpose.

﴿He has chosen you⟩. That is: He has chosen you for His religion and for supporting it, and no one else. In this is an indication of what requires striving and calls to it.

﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship⟩. That is: any constriction, by imposing what would be difficult for you to establish, indicating that there is no obstacle for them in it and no excuse for them in abandoning it. Or it refers to the concession (rukhsa) in neglecting some of what He commanded them where it would be difficult for them, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If I command you with something, then do of it what you are able." It is said that this means He made for them a way out of every sin, by granting them concessions in tight situations, opening for them the door of repentance, and legislating for them expiations (kaffarat) for the rights of Allah and compensations (arsh) and blood-money (diyat) for the rights of the servants.

﴿The religion of your father Abraham⟩. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), governed by a verb implied by the meaning of what precedes it, with the omission of the modified noun; that is: He has expanded your religion with the expansion of the religion of your father Abraham. Or it is in the accusative by incitement (igra'), or by specification (ikhtisas). He is called their father because he is the father of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he is like a father to his community, in that he is the cause of their eternal life and of their existence in a manner that is considered worthy in the Hereafter. Or because most of the Arabs were from his offspring (ﷺ), so they were given precedence over others.

﴿He named you Muslims before⟩ in the earlier scriptures, ﴿and in this⟩, that is: in the Qur'an. The pronoun refers to Allah, the Exalted, and this is supported by the reading: "Allah named you." Or it refers to Abraham. Their being named Muslims in the Qur'an, though not from him (ﷺ), was on account of his naming them before in His saying: ﴿And from our offspring a Muslim community for You⟩. It is said that ﴿and in this⟩ has an implied complement: and in this is the explanation of His naming you Muslims.

﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you⟩ on the Day of Resurrection, connected with "He named you." ﴿That he has conveyed to you⟩, so this indicates the acceptance of his testimony for himself, relying on his infallibility; or by obedience to those who obeyed and disobedience of those who disobeyed.

﴿And that you may be witnesses over the people⟩ by conveying the messages of the Messengers to them.

﴿So establish prayer and give zakat⟩. That is: draw near to Allah through all kinds of acts of obedience, and their being singled out for mention is due to their excellence and virtue.

﴿And hold fast to Allah⟩. That is: trust in Him in all your affairs, and do not seek help or support except from Him.

﴿He is your Protector⟩: your helper and the one who manages your affairs.

﴿An excellent Protector and an excellent Helper⟩. He is, since there is no equal to Him in protection and support, (p-123) rather there is no true protector and no true helper other than Him, Mighty and Majestic.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Hajj is given the reward of a pilgrimage he performed and an umrah he performed, equal to the number of those who performed Hajj and Umrah in the past and in the future."
